docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The NASA Glenn Research Center publishes multiple aeronautics simulators available for free use by the public.

One simulator useful to understanding airfoils is the FoilSim Student Airfoil Interactive simulator (local) (NASA)

With this simulator you can investigate how an aircraft wing produces lift and drag by changing the values of different factors that affect lift and the factors that affect drag.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Collegiate Wind Competition (CWC) challenges undergraduate university students to design, test, and build transportable wind turbines. Alongside turbine design, multidisciplinary teams create business plans and engage in local outreach to prepare for careers in the booming renewable energy industry.

Teams publish their design reports as part of the competition, which can be a valuable source for research and inspiration. A collection of reports from winning teams in recent years and entries from Northern Arizona University can be found here.

docs.title: Download Airfoil Profile Data
docs.text:
On the Airfoil Tools site:

  1. Search for your chosen profile(s).
  2. Find the link for the Selig format dat file. Don’t click the link!
  3. Right click the Selig format dat file link and select Save Link As…
  4. Add .dat to the end of the filename and save it to your computer.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
1. Download the Airfoil DAT Importer Fusion Add-in .zip file1.
  2. Locate the downloaded .zip file with Finder. It will likely be in your Downloads folder.
  3. Double-click the .zip file. It will unpack the contents to a new folder.
  4. Start a new design in Fusion.
  5. Click UTILITIES, then Scripts and Add Ins.
  6. Click +, then Script or add-in from device.
  7. Single-click the folder that was created in step 3 to select it. IMPORTANT: Do not double click the folder and select any files inside it. The folder itself must be selected!
  8. Click Open.
  9. Find the name RC CAD Airfoil Dat Importer in the list. Turn the Run toggle switch ON, and check the Run on Startup box as shown below.

docs.title: Import the Airfoil Data
docs.text:
1. Turn on the Origin view.
  2. Select Import Airfoil from the Create menu.

Note: if you don’t see this menu item, complete the Install Plug-in section of this guide first.

3. Import the airfoil data: 1. Click Browse… and select the .dat file you downloaded. 2. Choose a Chord Length. Something in the range of about 30-60 mm is about right for the size we will build, but this is your option. 3. Select one of the Origin planes in your design to create a new sketch on. 4. Click OK.

A new sketch is created in your design with points from the airfoil data file.

  1. Locate and edit the new sketch. You might need to click the > to expand the Sketches category.

docs.title: Option: No Taper
docs.text: Simply extrude the profile to the blade length you want.

docs.title: Option: Tapered
docs.text:
1. Select the Offset Plane tool.
  2. Select the same plane on the origin that the first sketch was drawn on.
  3. Drag the plane to your desired blade length.
  4. Repeat the earlier steps to import airfoil data:
  5. Creating the new sketch on the offset plane
  6. Choose a smaller chord length
  7. Edit the new sketch to close the shape as required

You should now have two sketches with different sizes of airfoil shapes.

  1. Select the Loft tool.
  2. Click to select the first airfoil profile, then the second. The loft tool will interpolate between them. Because the second profile had a different chord length than the first, the final object will be tapered as seen from above, reducing the mass of the blade from root to tip.

docs.title: Option: Blended Airfoil Profiles
docs.text: You can use more than one airfoil design. Repeat the above steps, but use a different airfoil profile for the second sketch. The Loft tool will blend them.

docs.title: Option: Twist
docs.text:
You can gradually twist the airfoil from root to tip to better adjust for the slower airspeed near the root to the faster airspeed near the tip.

  • Repeat the above steps, creating multiple offset planes along the length of the blade.
  • Rotate each sketch profile around a point that is approximately 25% from the front of the blade.
  • Select all the profiles for the Loft tool.

  1. Source: RC CAD LLC ↩

docs.title: Expected Wind Speed
docs.text:
Ms. Dooley and Mr. Willis measured the wind speed in Willow Bend’s wind tunnel, which will likely be used at the competition.

At the center of the tunnel (24 inches from the front, 24 inches off the ground, and centered left-to-right), we measured 4.1 meters per second with the fans on medium speed (the speed we tested our kits at) and 4.0 meters per second with the fans on high speed (yes, it was slower!).

docs.title: Collect Performance Data
docs.text:
We are only interested in performance data for low wind speeds (low Reynolds numbers). On the Airfoil Tools site:

  1. Uncheck boxes for any Reynolds numbers above 100,000 and click the Update plots button.
  2. Create a screenshot of the Cl v Alpha plot for your team’s documentation.

A CL vs. alpha (α) plot shows how much lift an airfoil produces at different angles.

  • CL (coefficient of lift) \= how much lift the blade makes
  • Alpha (α) \= the angle between the wind and the blade

Steps to Use the Plot

  1. Find the peak (before stall) Look for the highest point on the graph before it drops off. This is where the airfoil makes the most efficient lift.

  2. Choose a good operating angle Don’t pick the very top—choose a slightly lower angle (often \~4°–8°). This avoids stall and keeps the blade stable.

  3. Set your blade pitch Use that angle to decide how much to twist your blade in your design.

  4. Adjust from root to tip

  • Near the hub (root): larger angle

  • Near the tip: smaller angle This helps the whole blade work efficiently.

Key Idea

You are using the graph to pick the best angle for your blade to “slice” through the air and generate lift without stalling.

docs.title: Connect4
docs.text:
You will not be playing Connect 4 in this assignment. You'll be writing a Python library that plays it for you — and then entering your library in a tournament against every other library in the room. Your code takes the turns. You get to watch.

ChatGPT drew this image. The locations of the pieces don't make sense based on the rules (below), but it looks nice!

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll build a Python library — a module of functions — that plays Connect 4 on behalf of one player automatically: proposing moves, checking the legality of an opponent's moves, and detecting wins and ties. The functions must match the required signatures precisely, because a tournament program will be calling them without you there to explain what you meant.

Builds on: 2D Lists Tic-Tac-Toe — you'll reuse representing a game board as a 2D list and checking it for wins.

You've got it when…

  • Your library file is named your first name, all lowercase.
  • All four required functions exist with the exact signatures below.
  • check_move correctly accepts legal moves and rejects illegal ones.
  • check_win correctly reports "WIN", "TIE", or "IN PROGRESS".
  • make_move always returns a legal column, for any board it is given.
  • Your functions recover gracefully when passed illegal arguments.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. This is a competition — helping an opponent build their library is a bold strategy.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: The tournament measures your algorithm against theirs. Design it, write it, and test it yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: The Game
docs.text:
Connect 4 is a two-player strategy game played on a vertical grid with 7 columns and 6 rows. Players take turns dropping one colored disc at a time into any column. The disc falls to the lowest available space in that column.

The goal is simple: Be the first player to form a straight line of four of your own discs.

A winning line of four can be:

  • Horizontal (left–right)
  • Vertical (up–down)
  • Diagonal (either direction)

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. Players take turns one at a time.
  2. On your turn, drop one piece into any column you want.
  3. You can't take pieces out once they're in the board.
  4. The first person to get four in a row wins!
  5. If the whole board fills up and nobody has four in a row, it's a tie.

docs.title: Your Mission
docs.text: You will create a Python library to play Connect4 on behalf of one player automatically. Your library will play against other students' libraries!

docs.title: The Game State
docs.text:
The game board will be represented by a 2D list. Spaces will either be "-" for an empty space, "R" for a red piece, or "Y" for a yellow piece. Here are examples of this data structure.

Creation of an empty game board:

state = [
    ["-", "-", "-", "-", "-", "-", "-"],
    ["-", "-", "-", "-", "-", "-", "-"],
    ["-", "-", "-", "-", "-", "-", "-"],
    ["-", "-", "-", "-", "-", "-", "-"],
    ["-", "-", "-", "-", "-", "-", "-"],
    ["-", "-", "-", "-", "-", "-", "-"],
]

An empty game board (text, as it would be printed to the screen):

-------
-------
-------
-------
-------
-------

A game in progress (text, as it would be printed to the screen):

-------
-------
-------
R------
R-Y----
RYRY---

A win for red (text, as it would be printed to the screen):

-------

docs.title: Assignment
docs.text:
Create a library. It must follow these rules precisely:

  1. Your library file shall be named your first name, all lowercase letters. Example: steve.py

  2. Create a function with this exact signature:

    def make_move(piece, state):

    This function shall accept two arguments:

    • piece: a string representing your piece, either "R" or "Y".
    • state: the game board state as described in the previous section.

    This function shall return an int with the column your program chooses to play. It must be in the range 0 through 6.

  3. Create a function with this exact signature:

    def check_move(piece, column, state):

    This function shall accept three arguments:

    • piece: a string representing a piece to be played, either "R" or "Y".
    • column: an int representing the column to be played, 0 through 6.
    • state: the game board state before making this move as described in the previous section.

    This function shall return True if the proposed move is legal, or False otherwise.

  4. Create a function with this exact signature:

    def check_win(state):

    This function shall accept one argument:

    • state: the game board state as described in the previous section.

    This function shall return one of these strings exactly as spelled here:

    • "WIN" if a win has occurred
    • "TIE" if a tie has occurred
    • "IN PROGRESS" if the game is still in play

  5. Create a function with this exact signature:

    def get_name():

    This function shall return your first name as a string, properly capitalized.

Warning

"Precisely" means precisely. The tournament program calls your functions by these exact names and argument lists, and expects the exact return values described. A misspelled function name or a return value of "win" instead of "WIN" doesn't earn partial credit — it forfeits games.

docs.title: Tournament Flow
docs.text:
• Your library will play against other students' libraries in a tournament.
  • Two players are randomly matched for a game.
  • A program, which will be provided for you at the time of the tournament, will provide the following flow:

On your turn:

  1. The program calls your make_move() function.
  2. The program then calls your opponent's check_move() on your proposed move.
    • If your move is illegal and your opponent correctly flags it, you lose.
  3. If the move is legal, the game state is updated with your move.
  4. The program calls your check_win() function.
    • If you do not return a valid result string (as defined above), you lose.
    • If your move actually wins the game and you correctly report this, you win.
  5. The program then calls your opponent's check_win() function.
    • If your move really won the game, you failed to report it, and your opponent correctly reports it, your opponent wins.
    • If your move tied the game, you failed to report it, and your opponent correctly reports it, your opponent wins.

Play continues with alternating turns until someone wins (or a tie is correctly reported).

Referees who play, players who referee

Notice that your library is never trusted to referee itself. Your opponent's check_move and check_win are watching every move you make, and yours are watching theirs. A library with a sharp check_win can win games its make_move didn't earn — an opponent that fails to report its own victory hands the game to you.

docs.title: Test Cases
docs.text:
Your library should include a main() function that thoroughly tests each of your three game functions: make_move(), check_move(), and check_win(). (We'll take get_name() on faith.) You must think of test cases that show your function will recover gracefully from illegal arguments being passed to it.

Your main() function must be protected like this:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Why the protection?

Code guarded by if __name__ == "__main__": runs only when your file is run directly — not when the tournament program imports it as a library. Without the guard, your tests would run in the middle of the tournament, which is not the kind of surprise that helps you.

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text:
• A detailed description of your algorithm for your make_move() function. You must describe the process your code will use for choosing a column based on the game state. This should not include any Python code!
  • Your library Python (.py) file, named exactly as required above.

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent All four functions exist with the exact required signatures in a file named your lowercase first name; check_move and check_win are correct and recover gracefully from illegal arguments; your make_move algorithm description is precise enough that another programmer could implement it without asking you anything — and contains no Python code. 3 — Above Average The library is complete and tournament-ready with a minor slip — an edge case check_win misses, or an algorithm description that skips a detail your code actually handles. 2 — Average The functions exist but one misbehaves (a win direction never detected, illegal moves accepted), or the algorithm description reads like Python with the punctuation removed. 1 — Below Average Required functions missing or misspelled, signatures that don't match, or a library that crashes when the tournament calls it. 0 — Failing Nothing turned in, or a file the tournament program can't even import.

docs.title: Merge Sort
docs.text: Your card-sorting algorithm worked one card at a time. Merge sort refuses to sort anything at all — it just splits the list in half, hands each half to another copy of itself, and lets a one-item list count as sorted. That sounds like dodging the work. It's actually one of the fastest sorting algorithms ever devised, and after the Mondrian lab, you already know its secret: it's recursion.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Concept: Break the list into smaller pieces, sort those pieces, then combine them back together in order.

  1. Divide: Recursively split the unsorted list into two halves until each sublist contains only one element.
  2. Conquer: A single-element list is considered sorted.
  3. Combine (Merge): Repeatedly merge the sorted sublists back together to produce new sorted sublists until only one remains.

Builds on: Recursion — the same split-and-recurse pattern that painted Mondrians, now sorting lists.

You've got it when…

  • Your merge function combines two sorted lists into one sorted list.
  • Your merge_sort function sorts any list by calling itself, then calling merge.
  • You've tested both functions — including odd-length lists, an empty list, and a list of one item.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. Compare test results with a neighbor, not code.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Implementing an algorithm from its description is the whole assignment. Follow the steps below yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Part 1: The Merge Sort Process
docs.text:
1. If the list has one item or fewer, it is already sorted — return the list.
  2. Find the middle of the list.
  3. Split the list into two halves: a left half and a right half.
  4. Sort the left half using merge sort.
  5. Sort the right half using merge sort.
  6. Merge the two sorted halves back together (see Part 2 below).
  7. Return the merged list.

Steps 4 and 5 are the recursion

"Sort the left half using merge sort" — the algorithm you are writing calls itself, just like subdivide did. Step 1 is its stopping condition, and it's why the whole thing ends: every split eventually produces lists of one item, and those come back immediately.

docs.title: Part 2: How to Merge Two Sorted Lists
docs.text:
You are given two already sorted lists (left and right).

  1. Create an empty list called result.
  2. Set two positions: i for the left list and j for the right list, both starting at 0.
  3. Repeat while both lists still have items left:
    1. Compare the current items, left[i] and right[j].
    2. If left[i] is smaller: add it to result and move i forward.
    3. Otherwise: add right[j] to result and move j forward.
  4. If there are remaining items in the left list, add all of them to result.
  5. If there are remaining items in the right list, add all of them to result.
  6. Return result.

Why merging is the easy part

Both lists arrive sorted, so the smallest unclaimed item is always sitting at the front of one list or the other. Merging never searches — it just compares the two front items and takes the smaller one, like two checkout lines feeding one door.

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
Implement the merge sort algorithm in Python.

How to tackle this? Tips:

  1. Write the merge part first (Part 2 above).

    Start with a function that accepts two lists, left and right:

    def merge(left, right):
    • This function should return a new list with the two lists merged in sorted order.
    • Follow the steps in Part 2 of the algorithm above to write this function.

  2. Test your merge function with small lists.

    What does a good merge test look like?

    Feed it two short sorted lists by hand — say [2, 5, 9] and [1, 5, 6] — and check the output against what you'd expect. Then try uneven lengths and an empty list on one side.

  3. Now write a merge sort function (Part 1 above).

    This function accepts a list of items to sort:

    def merge_sort(input_list):
    • This function will call your merge function.
    • Follow the steps in Part 1 of the algorithm above to write this function.

Warning

Merge sort functions return their results — merge_sort hands back a new sorted list rather than rearranging the one you gave it. Forgetting a return (in steps 1 or 7 of Part 1, or step 6 of Part 2) is the most common way this lab produces a program that runs fine and sorts nothing.

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text: • Your Python (.py) file with your merge and merge_sort functions.

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent merge combines two sorted lists correctly and merge_sort sorts by calling itself and then merge — both return their results — and your file shows the tests that prove it, including odd-length lists, an empty list, and a list of one. 3 — Above Average Both functions work; an edge case went untested, or a test that exists in your head but not in the file. 2 — Average merge works but merge_sort doesn't — usually a missing return, the bug that runs fine and sorts nothing. 1 — Below Average Neither function produces sorted output. 0 — Failing No file turned in.

docs.title: Traveling Salesman
docs.text: Every algorithm in this unit has had an exact answer waiting at the end. This lab is the exception — a problem so expensive to solve exactly that with just 30 cities, checking every route would outlast the universe. Time to meet the workaround the real world runs on.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll play the Traveling Salesman Game: visit every city once and return home by the shortest route you can find. Along the way you'll discover why "just check every path" stops being an option almost immediately, and you'll design your own heuristics — rules of thumb that trade a guaranteed-best answer for one that's good enough, fast enough.

Builds on: Merge Sort — the end of the unit's tour of exact algorithms, and the reason this lab needs a different tool entirely.

Play the Traveling Salesman Game

You've got it when…

  • You've tied or beaten the computer's distance on a 5-city game.
  • You can say how many possible paths 5 cities and 30 cities each have — and what that means for solving by brute force.
  • You've written two different heuristics and played a 30-city game with each.
  • You can argue whether your heuristics were "good enough," and for what.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. Comparing routes and heuristics with your neighbors afterward is encouraged — that's the point of the Consider questions.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Your rule of thumb, your routes. What the levels mean.

Recording your answers

Answers and screenshots for the numbered questions below go in your notebook.

docs.title: Starting Small
docs.text:
1. Set the number of cities to 5.

  2. Click on a city of your choice to start with (any dot).

  3. Click a second dot, then a third, and so on to create a path between the cities.

  4. Visit each city only once.

  5. Complete the path by returning to the first city.

  6. Play until you tie or beat the distance to beat shown at the bottom of the screen.

    Note: it is unlikely that you will find a shorter path than the computer with only 5 cities…just try to tie!

    Your screen should look like this.

  7. Question: how many possible paths are there to explore between 5 cities?

  8. Paste a screenshot of your tie/win in your notebook.

docs.title: Scaling Up
docs.text:
We have worked with a number of algorithms, which are exact, step-by-step solutions. Some problems cannot be solved with algorithms. For those problems, we use heuristics, a practical shortcut or rule of thumb that:

  • Aims for a good (but not guaranteed optimal) solution
  • Is often used when exact solutions are too slow or complex
  • May sacrifice accuracy for speed or simplicity

  1. Set the number of cities to 30.

  2. How many possible paths are there to explore between 30 cities?

    Stuck? Open for a hint.

    From your starting city you can go to any of the 29 others, then any of the remaining 28, and so on. Multiply it out — or look up the factorial function on your calculator — and compare the result to, say, the number of seconds since the universe began.

  3. Write a heuristic — a simple rule that you will use to decide which city you will visit next from any city you are currently at.

    (Bad) example: "I will always visit the farthest unvisited city from my current city."

  4. Follow your heuristic to play one 30-city game and paste a screenshot in your notebook.

  5. Write a second heuristic that tries a different approach.

  6. Follow your heuristic to play one 30-city game and paste a screenshot in your notebook.

Warning

Follow your heuristic literally, even when your eyes can see it's about to make a bad choice. The moment you override it with human judgment, you're no longer measuring the heuristic — and a computer following your rule wouldn't get to cheat.

Consider:

  • Did either of your heuristics beat the computer?
  • Is the computer guaranteed to have the shortest possible path?
  • Is your heuristic "good enough"? Would you be happy with it if you were paying for gas to drive between these cities or the airline tickets to fly between them?

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text:
• Your answers to questions 7, 10, 11, and 13, in your notebook.
  • Your three game screenshots (steps 8, 12, and 14), in your project notebook.
  • Your thoughts on the three Consider questions, in your project notebook.

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent Path counts for 5 and 30 cities computed with visible reasoning (not guessed), two genuinely different heuristics written as rules a computer could follow, all three screenshots in the notebook, and Consider answers that argue "good enough" using your own routes as the evidence. 3 — Above Average Everything present; the two heuristics are near-duplicates, or a path count is right without the reasoning. 2 — Average One heuristic played instead of two, or screenshots missing — the games happened but the evidence didn't. 1 — Below Average Screenshots with no written answers, or answers with no games played. 0 — Failing Nothing in the notebook.

docs.title: Connect4 Check Win Helper Functions
docs.text: A Connect 4 board has 69 possible winning lines, and your check_win function has to notice every one of them. Checking them all in one giant function is possible, in the same way that eating a pizza in one bite is possible. Instead, we'll write one small helper function per direction and let check_win call them.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll write four helper functions — one for each way a player can win: horizontal, vertical, and the two diagonals. Each one answers a single, narrow question: is this location the start of a four-in-a-row? Your check_win function can then scan the board asking that question at every location.

Builds on: Connect4 — these helpers become part of your library from that assignment.

You've got it when…

  • is_horiz_win returns True exactly when a horizontal four-in-a-row starts at the given row and column.
  • You have working is_vert_win, is_diag_descending_win, and is_diag_ascending_win functions built the same way.
  • Each function returns False (instead of crashing) when asked about a location too close to the board's edge.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own — this code competes in the tournament.

docs.title: The Horizontal Helper
docs.text:
Let's create a helper function to help with the check_win function. This one will check if a given location (row and column) is the first of a horizontal win.

  1. Add this function to your Connect4 library file.

    def is_horiz_win(state, row, col):
    # Check the bounds...don't fall off the board!
    if row < 0 or row > 5:
        return False
    if col < 0 or col > 3:
        return False

    # Gather the pieces
    piece1 = state[row+0][col+0]
    piece2 = state[row+0][col+1]
    piece3 = state[row+0][col+2]
    piece4 = state[row+0][col+3]

    # If the first piece is blank, no win
    if piece1 == "-":
        return False

    # If all four pieces are the same (and they can't be blanks), it is a win.
    return piece1 == piece2 == piece3 == piece4

Why does col stop at 3?

A horizontal win reads four pieces to the right of its starting location. Starting at column 4, 5, or 6 would run off the edge of a 7-column board, so those columns can never be the start of a horizontal win. The bounds check refuses them up front, and the row+0/col+0 arithmetic is written out so you can see exactly which direction each helper walks.

docs.text:
Now copy and paste the helper function above and modify it to create these additional functions:

  1. Create is_vert_win:

    def is_vert_win(state, row, col):

  2. Create is_diag_descending_win:

    def is_diag_descending_win(state, row, col):

  3. Create is_diag_ascending_win:

    def is_diag_ascending_win(state, row, col):
Stuck? Open for a hint.

Only two things change between directions: the bounds that keep the four pieces on the board, and the offsets used to gather them. A vertical win walks down the rows (row+1, row+2, row+3) while the column stays put — so which index needs the tighter bound now? The diagonals change both indexes at once, and the ascending diagonal walks one of them backwards.

docs.title: Connect4 Check Move Hints
docs.text: Your check_move function is the referee's whistle: in the tournament, it's what catches an opponent's illegal move and wins you the game on the spot. The good news is that a Connect 4 move can only be illegal in a few ways, and each one is a quick check.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This is a fairly straightforward function with a signature that looks like this:

def check_move(piece, column, state):

We're checking whether a proposed move is legal. In other words, if someone holding piece wants to drop it in column and the game board looks like state, is that allowed?

Builds on: Connect4 Check Win Helper Functions — same library, next function.

You've got it when…

  • check_move rejects columns that don't exist on the board.
  • check_move rejects moves into full columns.
  • check_move rejects moves that would break the piece-count balance.
  • Every other move comes back True.

Collaboration & AI

docs.title: The Checks
docs.text:
Let's go through the logic for some checks:

  1. At any time, there are only 7 possible moves (columns 0 through 6). If column is less than 0 or greater than 6, the proposed move is illegal and we can return False immediately.

  2. If column is full, the proposed move is not legal. A shortcut to check if a column is full is to simply check if row 0 (the top row) has a blank "-" in the desired column. If not, the column must be full and the move is illegal; we can return False immediately.

    Tip

    Gravity does the bookkeeping for you. Pieces stack from the bottom, so the top row is always the last space to fill — if it's occupied, everything below it must be too. One comparison replaces a loop.

  3. There should always be either an equal number of each piece, or the count of each piece should differ by not more than one:

    1. Count all the red pieces.
    2. Count all the yellow pieces.
    3. Add piece to either the red or yellow count (whichever it is).
    4. If the absolute value of the difference between the red and yellow count is greater than one, the proposed move would be illegal and we can return False immediately.
    if abs(red_count - yellow_count) > 1:

    Why count pieces at all?

    Players alternate turns, so the piece counts can never drift more than one apart. A proposed move that would put red three pieces ahead means somebody is playing out of turn — and your referee should say so.

  4. Finally, if we can't find any of the above problems with the proposed move, it is legal, and we can return True.

docs.text: Before your library plays a single tournament game, you can find out whether it would survive one. The test program below throws 10,000 randomly-generated games and every possible winning line at your code — which is more scrutiny than your opponents will manage, and far better to face in private.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A unit test is a small, automated check that verifies one specific piece of code — usually a single function — behaves correctly for known inputs.

In short: unit tests test the smallest "units" of code in isolation.

A program that performs unit tests for your Connect4 assignment is provided below to help you detect any issues. These tests cannot guarantee that your assignment will run correctly in all cases! The intent is to detect typical errors before your final submission.

Builds on: Connect4 Check Move Hints — your library needs all four required functions before the tests mean much.

You've got it when…

  • The test program runs against your library file.
  • Every test reports PASS.

docs.title: The Test Program
docs.text:
test_connect4.py
"""
Utility for unit testing Connect4 library submissions.

To use this:
(1) Save this file to the same location as the module (library) file to test.
(2) Run this program. It finds your library file automatically.

Author: Steve Willis
Version: 1.2
"""

### DO NOT EDIT THIS FILE! ###

from contextlib import redirect_stdout, redirect_stderr
import copy
import importlib
import inspect
import io
import os
import random
import sys

ROWS = 6
COLS = 7

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
sys.path.insert(0, HERE)

MODULE_NAME = None  # set automatically by find_module_name()

def find_module_name():
    """Find the library to test: the only other .py file in this folder."""
    this_file = os.path.basename(__file__)
    candidates = [f[:-3] for f in sorted(os.listdir(HERE))
                  if f.endswith(".py") and f != this_file]
    if len(candidates) == 1:
        return candidates[0]
    if len(candidates) == 0:
        print("No library found to test!")
        print(f"Save your Connect4 .py file in this folder: {HERE}")
        return None
    print("More than one .py file is in this folder. Which is your library?")
    for i, name in enumerate(candidates):
        print(f"  ({i}) {name}.py")
    while True:
        choice = input("Enter a number: ")
        if choice.isdigit() and int(choice) < len(candidates):
            return candidates[int(choice)]

def empty_state():
    """Helper function to generate an empty game board."""
    return [["-" for j in range(COLS)] for i in range(ROWS)]

def tied_state():
    """Helper function to generate a tied game board."""
    row_a = list("RRRYRRR")
    row_b = list("YYYRYYY")
    return [row_a, row_b, row_a, row_b, row_a, row_b]

def rand_state():
    """Helper function to generate a random, reachable state with no winner."""
    def check_winner():
        directions = ((0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1), (1, -1))
        for r in range(ROWS):
            for c in range(COLS):
                p = state[r][c]
                if p not in ("R", "Y"):
                    continue
                for dr, dc in directions:
                    er, ec = r + 3 * dr, c + 3 * dc
                    if 0 <= er < ROWS and 0 <= ec < COLS:
                        if all(state[r + i * dr][c + i * dc] == p for i in range(4)):
                            return True
        return None

    y_count = 0
    r_count = 0
    state = empty_state()
    player = "R"
    moves = random.randint(0, ROWS * COLS - 1)  # number of moves to make
    heights = [0] * COLS  # how many pieces currently in each column (0..6)
    for _ in range(moves):
        legal_cols = [c for c in range(COLS) if heights[c] < ROWS]
        if not legal_cols:
            break

        c = random.choice(legal_cols)
        r = ROWS - 1 - heights[c]
        state[r][c] = player
        heights[c] += 1

        while check_winner():
            # take back the last (winning) move
            state[r][c] = "-"
            heights[c] -= 1
            legal_cols.remove(c)

            if len(legal_cols) > 0:
                c = random.choice(legal_cols)
                r = ROWS - 1 - heights[c]
                state[r][c] = player
                heights[c] += 1
            else:
                return state, player

        player = "Y" if player == "R" else "R"

    return state, player

def test_01_import():
    """The library imports without error"""
    if not os.path.exists(os.path.join(HERE, f"{MODULE_NAME}.py")):
        return f"{MODULE_NAME}.py does not exist"
    importlib.import_module(MODULE_NAME)
    return None

def test_02_has_required_functions():
    """The library contains all required functions with correct spelling"""
    required = {
        "get_name()",
        "check_move(piece, column, state)",
        "check_win(state)",
        "make_move(piece, state)"
    }
    module = importlib.import_module(MODULE_NAME)
    fns = inspect.getmembers(module, inspect.isfunction)
    sigs = {f"{name}{inspect.signature(obj)}" for name, obj in fns}
    missing = required - sigs
    return f"missing {', '.join(missing)}" if missing else None

def test_03_get_name():
    """get_name() returns a string with nonzero length"""
    module = importlib.import_module(MODULE_NAME)
    result = module.get_name()
    err = None
    if not isinstance(result, str):
        err = "did not return a string"
    elif len(result) < 1:
        err = "returned string is zero length"
    return err

def test_04_check_move_input():
    """check_move() accepts either a R or Y piece"""
    module = importlib.import_module(MODULE_NAME)
    r = module.check_move("R", 0, empty_state())
    y = module.check_move("Y", 0, empty_state())
    return "did not accept both piece types" if not all([r, y]) else None

def test_05_check_move_bounds():
    """check_move() rejects nonexistent columns"""
    module = importlib.import_module(MODULE_NAME)
    result_low = module.check_move("R", -1, empty_state())
    result_high = module.check_move("R", COLS, empty_state())
    err = None
    if not isinstance(result_low, bool) or not isinstance(result_high, bool):
        err = "wrong type returned"
    elif result_low or result_high:
        err = "allowed nonexistent column(s)"
    return err

def test_06_check_move_empty():
    """check_move() accepts moves into partially-filled columns"""
    module = importlib.import_module(MODULE_NAME)
    err = None

    # create a state with all but the top row filled with no winning combos
    state = [
        ["-", "-", "-", "-", "-", "-", "-"],
        ["R", "Y", "R", "Y", "R", "Y", "R"],
        ["Y", "R", "Y", "R", "Y", "R", "Y"],
        ["Y", "R", "Y", "R", "Y", "R", "Y"],
        ["R", "Y", "R", "Y", "R", "Y", "R"],
        ["R", "Y", "R", "Y", "R", "Y", "R"],
    ]

    # it is yellow's turn based on piece counts
    results = [module.check_move("Y", c, copy.deepcopy(state)) for c in range(COLS)]
    if not all(isinstance(r, bool) for r in results):
        err = "wrong type returned (expected True or False)"
    elif not all(results):
        err = "one or more partially-filled columns was not accepted"
    return err

def test_07_check_move_full():
    """check_move() rejects moves in full columns"""
    module = importlib.import_module(MODULE_NAME)
    err = None
    results = [module.check_move("R", c, tied_state()) for c in range(COLS)]
    if not all([isinstance(r, bool) for r in results]):
        err = "wrong type returned"
    elif any(results):
        err = "move allowed with full board"
    return err

def test_08_test_check_win_in_progress_empty():
    """check_win() detects a game is in progress (tested with empty board)."""
    module = importlib.import_module(MODULE_NAME)
    result = module.check_win(empty_state())

    if not isinstance(result, str):
        return "wrong type returned"
    if result not in ("WIN", "TIE", "IN PROGRESS"):
        return f"invalid response {result} (not WIN/TIE/IN PROGRESS)"
    if result != "IN PROGRESS":
        return f"incorrect response {result} (expected IN PROGRESS)"
    return None

def test_09_test_check_win_in_progress():
    """check_win() detects a game is in progress (tested with 1 - 41 pieces)."""
    module = importlib.import_module(MODULE_NAME)
    tied = tied_state()
    state = empty_state()

    # copy one piece at a time from the tied state to an initially empty state
    # from the bottom up.
    i = 0
    for r in reversed(range(ROWS)):
        for c in range(COLS):
            i += 1
            if i == 42: # don't test a 42nd piece...would be a tie
                return None

            state[r][c] = tied[r][c]
            result = module.check_win(state)

            if not isinstance(result, str):
                return "wrong type returned"
            if result not in ("WIN", "TIE", "IN PROGRESS"):
                return f"invalid response {result} (not WIN/TIE/IN PROGRESS)"
            if result != "IN PROGRESS":
                return f"incorrect response {result} (expected IN PROGRESS)"

def test_10_test_check_win_horiz():
    """check_win() detects all 24 possible horizontal wins"""
    count = 0
    module = importlib.import_module(MODULE_NAME)
    for r in range(ROWS):
        for c in range(COLS-3):
            state = empty_state()
            state[r][c] = state[r][c+1] = state[r][c+2] = state[r][c+3] = "R"
            result = module.check_win(state)
            if not isinstance(result, str):
                return "wrong type returned"
            if result not in ("WIN", "TIE", "IN PROGRESS"):
                return f"invalid response {result} (not WIN/TIE/IN PROGRESS)"
            if result == "WIN":
                count += 1
    return f"detected {count}/24 possible wins" if count != 24 else None

def test_11_test_check_win_vert():
    """check_win() detects all 21 possible vertical wins"""
    count = 0
    module = importlib.import_module(MODULE_NAME)
    for r in range(ROWS-3):
        for c in range(COLS):
            state = empty_state()
            state[r][c] = state[r+1][c] = state[r+2][c] = state[r+3][c] = "R"
            result = module.check_win(state)
            if not isinstance(result, str):
                return "wrong type returned"
            if result not in ("WIN", "TIE", "IN PROGRESS"):
                return f"invalid response {result} (not WIN/TIE/IN PROGRESS)"
            if result == "WIN":
                count += 1

    return f"detected {count}/21 possible wins" if count != 21 else None

def test_12_test_check_win_diag():
    """check_win() detects all 24 possible diagonal wins"""
    count = 0
    module = importlib.import_module(MODULE_NAME)
    # descending
    for r in range(ROWS-3):
        for c in range(COLS-3):
            st = empty_state()
            st[r][c] = st[r+1][c+1] = st[r+2][c+2] = st[r+3][c+3] = "R"
            result = module.check_win(st)
            if not isinstance(result, str):
                return "wrong type returned"
            if result not in ("WIN", "TIE", "IN PROGRESS"):
                return f"invalid response {result} (not WIN/TIE/IN PROGRESS)"
            if result == "WIN":
                count += 1

    # ascending
    for r in range(ROWS-3):
        for c in range(COLS-3):
            st = empty_state()
            st[r+3][c] = st[r+2][c+1] = st[r+1][c+2] = st[r][c+3] = "R"
            result = module.check_win(st)
            if not isinstance(result, str):
                return "wrong type returned"
            if result not in ("WIN", "TIE", "IN PROGRESS"):
                return f"invalid response {result} (not WIN/TIE/IN PROGRESS)"
            if result == "WIN":
                count += 1

    return f"detected {count}/24 possible wins" if count != 24 else None

def test_13_check_win_tie():
    """check_win() detects a tie/draw"""
    module = importlib.import_module(MODULE_NAME)
    state = tied_state()
    result = module.check_win(tied_state())
    if not isinstance(result, str):
        return "wrong type returned"
    if result not in ("WIN", "TIE", "IN PROGRESS"):
        return f"invalid response {result} (not WIN/TIE/IN PROGRESS)"
    elif result != "TIE":
        return f"incorrect response ({result}, expected TIE)"
    return None

def test_14_make_move_operation():
    """make_move() makes legal moves for 10,000 randomly-generated games"""
    n_tests = 10000
    tied = tied_state()
    count = 0
    for _ in range(n_tests):
        state, piece = rand_state()
        module = importlib.import_module(MODULE_NAME)
        result = module.make_move(piece, copy.deepcopy(state))
        if not isinstance(result, int):
            return f"wrong type returned after {count:,} legal moves"
        if 0 <= result < COLS and state[0][result] == "-":
            count += 1  # the move is legal
    if count != n_tests:
        return f"made {count:,} / {n_tests:,} legal moves"
    else:
        return None

def main():
    global MODULE_NAME
    MODULE_NAME = find_module_name()
    if MODULE_NAME is None:
        return

    print()
    print(f"Testing {MODULE_NAME}.py")
    print()
    print("HOW TO USE THIS TOOL")
    print("====================")
    print("Address any FAIL or ERROR results below from TOP TO BOTTOM!")
    print("A failure on an earlier test can cause failures on later tests.")
    print()

    current_module = sys.modules[__name__]
    fns = sorted(inspect.getmembers(current_module, inspect.isfunction))
    fns = [fn for name, fn in fns if name.startswith("test")]
    for test in fns:
        try:
            with OutputSuppressor():
                err = test()
        except:
            err = "program crashed while running test"

        result = "PASS" if not err else "FAIL"
        print(f"{result}: {test.__doc__}")
        if err:
            print(f"\t{err}")
    print()
    print("End of tests.")

class OutputSuppressor:
    """Context manager to suppress stdout/stderr."""
    def __enter__(self):
        self._stdout = io.StringIO()
        self._stderr = io.StringIO()
        self._out_cm = redirect_stdout(self._stdout)
        self._err_cm = redirect_stderr(self._stderr)
        self._out_cm.__enter__()
        self._err_cm.__enter__()
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        self._err_cm.__exit__(exc_type, exc, tb)
        self._out_cm.__exit__(exc_type, exc, tb)
        return False  # don't swallow exceptions

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Monty Hall Algorithm
docs.text: Three doors. One prize, two goats. You pick a door, the host opens a different one — always a goat — and offers to let you switch. Most people are certain that switching can't matter. Most people are wrong, and by the end of this lab your program will have proved it ten thousand times.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll learn to write an algorithm in natural language — a step-by-step solution in plain English, precise enough for someone else to follow exactly. Then you'll put the skill to work: write an algorithm for simulating the famous Monty Hall problem, and implement it as a Python program that settles the stay-or-switch argument with data.

Builds on: Unit Testing Your Connect4 Library — you described your make_move algorithm in words there; here we make that skill the whole point.

You've got it when…

  • Your natural language algorithm covers sequencing, selection, and iteration.
  • Another student could implement your algorithm without asking you questions.
  • Your program runs at least 10,000 simulated games and counts wins for both staying and switching.
  • Your printed results settle the question: does switching matter?

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. Trading algorithms with a neighbor to test whether they can follow yours is encouraged — that's the test that matters.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Describing a process precisely is the skill this lab builds. Write the words and the code yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Writing an Algorithm in Natural Language
docs.text:
Before writing code, programmers often describe their solution as a step-by-step set of instructions. This description is called an algorithm.

An algorithm written in natural language uses ordinary English sentences instead of programming syntax. Your goal is to describe the steps clearly enough that someone else could follow them exactly.

A good algorithm description contains three ingredients.

docs.title: Sequencing
docs.text:
Steps occur in a specific order. Example:

  1. Ask the user to enter a number.
  2. Multiply the number by 2.
  3. Display the result.

If the order changes, the outcome may change.

docs.title: Selection (Decision Making)
docs.text:
Sometimes the algorithm must choose between different actions depending on a condition. Natural language examples:

  • If the number is greater than 10, display "Large number".
  • Otherwise, display "Small number".

Selection usually uses words like if, otherwise, when, and unless.

docs.title: Iteration (Repeating Steps)
docs.text:
Sometimes a step must repeat multiple times. Natural language examples:

  • Repeat the following steps 5 times.
  • Continue asking for input until the user enters 0.
  • For each item in the list, print the item.

Iteration describes loops without using programming syntax.

docs.title: Writing Clear Steps
docs.text:
Each step should:

  • Start with an action verb
  • Describe exactly one action
  • Be clear and unambiguous

Good example:

  1. Ask the user for their age.
  2. Convert the input to a number.
  3. If the age is 18 or greater, display "Adult".
  4. Otherwise display "Minor".

Poor example:

Do something with the age and show the result.

The poor example is unclear and cannot be followed precisely.

Avoid programming syntax

Natural language algorithms should not look like code. Avoid things like:

if age >= 18:
    print("Adult")

Instead write: If the age is greater than or equal to 18, display "Adult".

Be precise

Imagine you are giving instructions to a very literal robot. "Get a number and do math with it" gets you nowhere. "Ask the user to enter a number. Multiply the number by 3. Add 5 to the result. Display the final value." gets you a program.

docs.title: Example Algorithm (Guessing Game)
docs.text:
Example written in natural language:

  1. Generate a random number between 1 and 10.
  2. Ask the user to guess the number.
  3. If the guess equals the random number, display "Correct!".
  4. Otherwise display "Try again."
  5. Repeat steps 2–4 until the user guesses correctly.
  6. Display the number of guesses the user made.

This algorithm includes sequencing (ordered steps), selection ("If the guess equals…"), and iteration ("Repeat steps…").

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
The Monty Hall Problem is a famous probability puzzle based on a game show scenario. In the game, a contestant chooses one of three doors. Behind one door is a prize, and behind the other two doors are goats.

After the contestant picks a door, the host — who knows where the prize is — opens one of the remaining doors that does not contain the prize. The contestant is then given a choice:

  • Stay with their original door, or
  • Switch to the remaining unopened door.

Many people believe that switching and staying are equally likely to win, but probability theory suggests otherwise.

Your task is to design an algorithm and then implement a simulation to test this claim.

docs.title: Part 1 — Write an Algorithm (Natural Language)
docs.text:
Before writing any code, write a step-by-step algorithm in natural language describing how to simulate the Monty Hall problem.

Your algorithm should include sequencing, selection (decisions such as which door the host opens), and iteration (repeating the simulation many times).

Your algorithm should clearly describe how to:

  1. Randomly place the prize behind one of three doors.
  2. Simulate the contestant selecting a door.
  3. Determine which door the host opens (a door that is not the prize and not the contestant's choice).
  4. Determine the result if the contestant stays with their original choice.
  5. Determine the result if the contestant switches to the remaining unopened door.
  6. Repeat the experiment many times (for example, 10,000 simulations).
  7. Count how many times each strategy wins.
  8. Display the results.

Your algorithm should be written so that another student could implement it directly.

Checklist before moving on

Ask yourself:

  • Are the steps in the correct order?
  • Is every step clear and specific?
  • Are decisions described using words like if or otherwise?
  • Are repeated actions clearly described?
  • Could another student follow the instructions exactly?

If the answer is yes, your algorithm is ready to be implemented in code.

docs.title: Part 2 — Implement the Simulation
docs.text:
Write a program that implements your algorithm.

Your program must:

  • Run a large number of trials (at least 10,000 recommended).
  • Track wins when the contestant stays and wins when the contestant switches.
  • Print the results.

Run your program. Your screen should look like this.

Total simulations: 10000
Wins when staying: 3345
Wins when switching: 6655

(Your counts will differ a little — it's random — but the ratio should tell a consistent story.) You may also display percentages if you wish.

This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent Your natural-language algorithm has all three ingredients — sequencing, selection, iteration — and is precise enough for another student to implement without questions; your program runs at least 10,000 trials, counts wins for both staying and switching, and the printed results settle the argument (roughly one third to two thirds). 3 — Above Average Both the algorithm and the working program are turned in, with a minor gap — one vague step, or output that reports numbers without labels. 2 — Average The algorithm or the program, but not both — or a simulation that runs but only counts one strategy. 1 — Below Average An algorithm that's really just code with the colons removed, or a program that doesn't run. 0 — Failing Nothing in the notebook and no program.

docs.title: Algorithm Extraction
docs.text: Last time you turned an algorithm into code. This lab runs the machine in reverse: you're handed four lines of working Python and asked to recover the algorithm hiding inside them. Working, that is, except when it isn't — there's a bug in here, and reading the code closely enough to extract its algorithm is exactly how you'll find it.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll read a short piece of code, describe its purpose in one sentence, imagine it as a function, write the algorithm it implements in natural language, and then find and fix the bug that makes it wrong for certain inputs.

Builds on: Monty Hall Algorithm — you'll use the same natural-language algorithm skills, pointed in the opposite direction.

You've got it when…

  • You can state the code's purpose in one sentence.
  • You've named the function, its parameters, and its return value.
  • Your extracted algorithm matches what the code actually does.
  • You've found the bug, named an input that triggers it, and fixed it.

Collaboration & AI

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Reading code without a tool explaining it to you is the skill under construction here. What the levels mean.

Recording your answers

Write your answers in your notebook, numbered to match the tasks below.

docs.text:

  3. Write the algorithm that this code implements.

  4. This code contains a bug and will produce an incorrect result with certain inputs. What is the bug?

    Stuck? Open for a hint.

    The bug isn't in the loop — it's in an assumption made before the loop starts. What inputs would make that assumption false? Try inventing lists of numbers until one produces an answer you know is wrong.

  5. Fix the bug. Write your corrected code in your notebook, and test it against the input that fooled the original.

docs.title: Search Algorithms
docs.text: Finding a name in a phone book by reading every entry from page one works, eventually. Opening to the middle and throwing away the wrong half each time works a few hundred times faster. Today you'll work both directions of the algorithm street: extract an algorithm from search code you're given, and build search code from an algorithm you're given.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll write the natural-language algorithm for linear search by reading its code, then implement binary search in Python by following its algorithm. Same two skills as the last two labs — extraction and implementation — applied to the two classic ways of finding things.

Builds on: Algorithm Extraction — extracting an algorithm from code, now paired with its opposite.

You've got it when…

  • Your linear search algorithm accurately describes what the code does, in plain English.
  • Your binary search program follows the given algorithm and finds a target in a sorted list.
  • Your program reports when the target is not in the list.
  • You've tested it: first item, last item, middle item, missing item.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. Compare algorithms with a neighbor after you've each written one.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Translating between code and algorithm — both directions — is the skill being built. Do the translating yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Linear Search
docs.text:
This code searches for a target number in a list of numbers.

numbers = [12, 7, 25, 3, 18, 42, 9]
target = 18

for i in range(len(numbers)):
    if numbers[i] == target:
        print("Found at index", i)
  1. Write the algorithm for this code in your notebook. Natural language, numbered steps — precise enough that someone who has never seen the code could rewrite it.

Why 'linear'?

Linear search checks every item, one at a time, front to back. The time it takes grows in a straight line with the length of the list — double the list, double the work. It's the only option when the list is in no particular order.

docs.title: Binary Search
docs.text:
This is the algorithm for binary search.

  1. Start with a sorted list of values.
  2. Set low to the first index of the list.
  3. Set high to the last index of the list.
  4. Repeat the following steps while low is less than or equal to high:
    1. Find the middle index: set middle to (low + high) // 2.
    2. Compare the middle value to the target:
      1. If the middle value equals the target: report the index and stop.
      2. If the target is less than the middle value: move the search to the left half — set high to middle - 1.
      3. If the target is greater than the middle value: move the search to the right half — set low to middle + 1.

  5. If the loop ends and the target was not found: report that the target is not in the list.

  6. Write and test a Python program that implements this algorithm.

Warning

Step 1 of the algorithm is not decoration. Binary search only works on a sorted list — the whole trick is knowing which half to throw away, and an unsorted list gives you no way to know. Test your program with a sorted list.

Stuck? Open for a hint.

The algorithm's step 4 is a while loop, and steps 4.1–4.2 live inside it. Notice that the algorithm stops when it reports success — in Python, break (or returning from a function) does that job.

docs.title: Sorting Introduction
docs.text: Binary search was a few hundred times faster than linear search — but it demanded a sorted list, and nobody said where sorted lists come from. They come from sorting algorithms, and you already run one every time you pick up a hand of cards. Today you'll figure out what it is you've been doing all along, and write it down.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Imagine you are holding a hand of playing cards that are not in order. You want to organize them from lowest to highest value (for example: 2 → 10 → Jack → Queen → King → Ace). You'll write a step-by-step algorithm in plain language that explains how you would sort the cards while holding them in your hand.

Builds on: Search Algorithms — binary search needed a sorted list; this is where sorted lists come from.

You've got it when…

  • Your algorithm is written in clear, complete sentences with numbered steps.
  • It covers every card in the hand, from the first to the last.
  • Another student could follow it exactly — with real cards — without asking you anything.
  • It stays within the constraints below.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. If you have a deck handy, testing your algorithm on a neighbor is fair play — watching them follow your words literally is the fastest way to find the gaps.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: The algorithm in your head is the one we're after. Write it down yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Recursion
docs.text: Piet Mondrian spent decades reducing painting to black lines and rectangles of red, blue, and yellow. You're going to reproduce his life's work with one function — a function whose defining trick is that it calls itself.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Piet Mondrian (1872–1944) was a Dutch artist. He is best known for his abstract paintings made of black grid lines and blocks of color, primarily red, blue, yellow, and white. His goal was to reduce art to its simplest visual elements and create balance through structure and proportion.

Composition A (1920) Tableau I (1921) Composition in Red, Yellow, Blue and Black (1921) Composition II in Red, Blue, and Yellow (1930)

Although Mondrian didn't use computers, his style connects surprisingly well to the idea of recursion in computer science.

In this assignment, you'll generate a Mondrian-style image by repeatedly subdividing a rectangle into smaller rectangles. This mirrors recursion because:

  • You start with one large rectangle
  • Apply the same rule: split it into smaller parts
  • Then apply that same rule again to each new rectangle

This "repeat the same process on smaller pieces" is exactly what recursion does.

So while Mondrian created his work by hand, your program will recreate a similar visual style using a recursive algorithm, turning an artistic idea into a computational one.

Builds on: Sorting Introduction — another algorithm implemented from a description; this one calls itself.

You've got it when…

  • Your program opens a window filled edge-to-edge with a Mondrian-style grid of colored rectangles.
  • Every run produces a different painting.
  • All of your code lives inside the subdivide function.
  • Changing the depth argument changes how finely the image is subdivided — and you can explain why.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. Compare paintings with your neighbors — no two should match.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Recursion has to click in your head, and it only clicks by writing one. Implement subdivide yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
1. Copy the code below to a new file in the Mu editor.

    import random

WIDTH = 800
HEIGHT = 600

mondrian_colors = ["white", "red", "blue", "yellow"]

rectangles = []

def draw():
    """ DO NOT CHANGE THIS FUNCTION """
    screen.fill((220, 220, 220))
    for item in rectangles:
        x, y, w, h, color = item
        r = Rect(x, y, w, h)
        screen.draw.filled_rect(r, color)
        screen.draw.rect(r, (0, 0, 0))

def subdivide(x, y, w, h, depth):
    """ YOUR CODE GOES HERE """

subdivide(0, 0, WIDTH, HEIGHT, 5)

  2. Change the Mu editor mode to Pygame Zero.

    1. Press the Mode button.
    2. Select Pygame Zero.

    Your screen should look like this.

  3. Implement the algorithm below in the body of the subdivide function. You should not edit anything outside of the subdivide function!

docs.title: The Algorithm
docs.text:
Inputs. The subdivide function is passed arguments/parameters describing a rectangular area on the screen:

  • x — the x-coordinate (left-right) of the upper-left corner of the rectangle
  • y — the y-coordinate (up-down) of the upper-left corner of the rectangle
  • w — the width of the rectangle
  • h — the height of the rectangle
  • depth — how deep the algorithm should go. We count this down each time subdivide is called recursively, and smaller and smaller rectangles will be created until it reaches zero.
  1. Check the stopping condition.
    • If depth is 0:
      • Choose a random color from the Mondrian color list.
      • Store a rectangle at (x, y) with the given width and height using that color. For this assignment, represent a rectangle as a tuple of (x, y, width, height, color). Append this tuple to the rectangles list.
      • Stop (do not continue).
  2. Decide how to split the rectangle.
    • If the width is greater than the height: split vertically.
    • Otherwise: split horizontally.
  3. Choose a split location.
    • Pick a random number between about 30% and 70% of the dimension being split.
  4. Create two smaller rectangles.
    • If splitting vertically:
      • Left rectangle: same y, height stays the same, width = split value.
      • Right rectangle: x starts at x + split, width = remaining width.
    • If splitting horizontally:
      • Top rectangle: same x, width stays the same, height = split value.
      • Bottom rectangle: y starts at y + split, height = remaining height.
  5. Repeat the process.
    • Call subdivide on each of the two new rectangles.
    • Decrease depth by 1 for each call.

Why the stopping condition comes first

A recursive function without a stopping condition is an infinite loop with better manners: each call spawns more calls, forever, until Python runs out of room to keep track of them all. Step 1 is what makes the whole thing land — the recursion drills down, hits depth 0, and starts actually storing rectangles.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Save your work first!

It is highly likely that Mu will crash during this step!

Try changing the depth argument on the last line of the program:

subdivide(0, 0, WIDTH, HEIGHT, 5)
  1. What happens as this number is increased?
  2. What limits how large you can make this number?
  3. What is the purpose of doing this task recursively? How would you go about doing this iteratively (with a loop) instead?

docs.title: Bubble Wand
docs.text: Let's write a program to design our own bubble wands!

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Instead of drawing a 3D model by hand, you'll write a program that builds one for you. In Tinkercad Codeblocks, each block adds, moves, or changes a shape, and pressing Play runs your program to draw the model. In this lab (Part One of two) you'll build the wand's blower ring, handle, and base — and wire the whole design to variables so one change can resize everything.

Before you start

You'll need your Tinkercad account login. Your design saves automatically to your account, and Part Two picks up right where this lab ends.

You've got it when…

  • Your wand has a blower ring, a handle, and a round base, all built from code blocks.
  • The shapes get their sizes from variables (InnerRadius, Thickness, OuterRadius, Overflow, and Length) instead of plain numbers.
  • Each section of your code starts with a comment saying what it builds.
  • The whole wand is one color.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. Ask a neighbor for a hand if you're stuck, but build your own wand.

docs.text: Our goal.

docs.text:
Your wand works, but it's smooth and a little thin. In this lab you'll use a loop to add a ring of ridges — the kind of repetitive job computers are built for — then thicken the whole wand by changing a single variable, and finally export the design as an .STL file ready for the 3D printer.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
The wand looks a bit fragile. Let's make it thicker everywhere. Instead of changing every piece, we can just set the variable once at the beginning of the program and the design will be updated everywhere that variable is used.

Try changing some other variables to customize your bubble wand!

docs.title: sk8board Time!
docs.text: Let's design and 3D print a fingerboard — a tiny skateboard we can skate with our fingers! We'll program it so that we can customize some of its features.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This build has more parts than the bubble wand: axles, trucks, a deck with curved kicks, and wheels that print separately and snap on. You'll set up variables named for real skateboard dimensions, then build each part by matching the block screenshots — the training wheels are off, so read each screenshot carefully and check your model as you go.

Builds on: Bubble Wand Part 2 — you'll reuse variables, math blocks, Group Selection, and exporting to .STL.

You've got it when…

  • Your model has two complete axle-and-truck assemblies, a deck with a kick at each end, and four separate wheels.
  • Your six variables control the board's dimensions.
  • Your design is exported as an .STL file and submitted.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. Ask a neighbor for a hand if you're stuck, but build your own board.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Reading the blocks is the skill this lab builds — do it with your own eyes. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: 1. Start a new Tinkercad Codeblocks project.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
1. Create these variables and set them to these values. We can change these later to customize our board!

    Here's what they will do:

    • width will be the width of the skateboard
    • deck length will be the length of the flat part of the deck
    • kick length will be the length of the curved nose and tail of the deck
    • wheelbase will be the distance between the wheels from front to back
    • wheel outer diameter and wheel inner diameter will control the size of the wheels

docs.title: Trucks and Axles
docs.text:
Axles are what the wheels spin on. Trucks mount the axles to the skateboard. We'll make these as one piece.

  1. Add a couple of toruses. Each wheel will snap on and ride between them.

    Notice the second torus is created with the Copy block to make a copy of the first torus, then moves it downward.

  2. Add a couple of boxes as holes. We'll use these to cut slits in the ends of the axles to make it easier to snap the wheel on.

    Notice that the second box is created with the Copy block to make a copy of the first box, then is rotated 90 degrees to make an 'X' with the first box.

  3. We have what we need for one wheel. There are two wheels on each axle. Let's copy what we've made so far and rotate it around for the other side of the axle.

  4. Next we'll add the axle itself.

  5. Now we'll add a bigger cylinder and triangle in the center of the axle to mount the axle to the underside of the skateboard. This is called a truck.

  6. Group the selection to apply the cut slits to the ends of the axle and move the axle into position to be the front axle.

  7. Make a copy of the front axle and move it into position to be the rear axle.

    Your model should look like this.

docs.title: Deck
docs.text:
Now we'll build the deck, which is the part of the skateboard that the skater stands on.

  1. Add the flat portion of the deck and move it into position.

  2. Now add a "kick" for the nose, which is the part of the deck that curves upward on the front of the board.

  3. Add the back kick by copying the front kick and rotating it around to the back of the deck.

    Your model should look like this.

docs.title: Wheels
docs.text:
Finally, we'll design some wheels. These will print as separate pieces to snap on to the axles.

  1. We'll add a Tube and move it into position, repeating four times to create four wheels.

    Your model should look like this.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent Your submitted .STL has both axle-and-truck assemblies with the snap-on slits, a deck with a kick at each end, and four separate wheels — and the six variables genuinely drive the design, so changing width or wheelbase rebuilds the board to match. 3 — Above Average A complete board is submitted with a minor mismatch — a kick rotated slightly off, a wheel overlapping an axle, or one dimension hard-coded where a variable belongs. 2 — Average Real gaps — one axle instead of two, no kicks, or missing wheels; or the variables exist at the top but the shapes below don't use them. 1 — Below Average A few shapes that don't yet resemble a skateboard, or nothing exported. 0 — Failing Nothing submitted and no design in your account.

docs.title: Spinning Top Battle
docs.text: Your challenge is to design a spinning top to battle with others!

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
No step-by-step instructions this time. You've built a bubble wand and a fingerboard from code blocks — now you'll design something entirely your own, within the size limits, and print it to face the other tops in class. The last one spinning wins.

Builds on: sk8board Time! — every Codeblocks skill you've picked up in this unit is fair game.

You've got it when…

  • Your top is designed in Tinkercad Codeblocks.
  • It fits the size limits: no more than 40 millimeters across and 50 millimeters tall.
  • It has at least one feature you chose on purpose to help it battle.
  • Your .STL file is submitted for printing.

Collaboration & AI

Work: Your own design — that's the point of a battle. Researching other designs is encouraged; copying a classmate's isn't.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Design and build the top yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Your Mission
docs.text:
Do this:

  1. Research some spinning top designs on the internet. Try searching for "spinning top" or "3D printed spinning top".

  2. Create your design in Tinkercad Codeblocks.

    • You can equip your top with any features you think will help it battle other tops.

    Size limits

    Your top should not be larger than 40 millimeters in diameter (20 millimeters in radius) or 50 millimeters tall. A top that's too big for the printer doesn't battle anyone.

  3. Submit your .STL file for printing.

Stuck for ideas?

Think about what makes a top spin long and hit hard: where the weight sits, how low it rides, and what its edge does when it meets another top. Physics is on the team of whoever thinks about it first.

docs.text: • Your spinning top's .STL file, submitted for printing.

docs.title: How It's Graded
