docs.title: Organization With a List Data Structure
docs.text:
1. Read the following EarSketch Curriculum sections and apply them to your song.

    • Section 9.1
    • Section 9.2

  2. Store all the sounds your song uses in a list. See examples in Section 9.1.

  3. Use a loop to access the sounds in your list and add them to your song with fitMedia(). See examples in Section 9.1.

  4. Use information from Section 9.2 to call makeBeat() with a list to handle multiple sounds at once (see the final example code in this section).

docs.title: Grading Rubric
docs.text: Item Points All sounds stored in a list 20% Loop used to add sounds from the list with fitMedia() 40% makeBeat() called with a list of sounds 40%

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text:
Download your script from EarSketch and submit it:

  1. Click the toggle switch to expand the Content Manager.

  2. Select the SCRIPTS tab.

  3. Find your song's script in the MY SCRIPTS panel and click its Download button .

  4. Click the download button next to the Script option.

  5. Submit the downloaded Python (.py) file in Google Classroom.

  • Your song's script (.py file) submitted in Google Classroom.

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent Every sound the song uses lives in one list, a loop feeds them to fitMedia(), and makeBeat() takes a list to run multiple sounds at once — with no orphaned sound variables left behind from the old way. 3 — Above Average All three requirements met; a sound or two still lives outside the list. 2 — Average The list exists, but the loop or the list-powered makeBeat() doesn't use it. 1 — Below Average Sounds are still individual variables end to end. 0 — Failing Nothing submitted in Google Classroom.

docs.title: EarSketch: Function Return and Boolean Logic
docs.text: Your functions build sections of your song, but so far the conversation is one-way: you call them, they work, they say nothing back. In this lab your functions return answers the rest of the program can use — and your song learns to take requests.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
We will write functions that return useful values, use those values in the main program, and let a user customize the song with input and boolean logic — expressions that are either True or False.

Before you start

Open your song script in EarSketch. This lab continues the song you've been building.

You've got it when…

  • At least one of your functions returns a value.
  • The main program uses that return value in a meaningful way.
  • A user can customize the song by answering a prompt, and boolean logic changes the song based on the answer.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. You'll need a neighbor as a test user — their job is to answer the prompts, not to fix your code.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Return values and boolean logic are the last fundamentals of the unit. Finish them yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Return Values, User Input, and Boolean Logic
docs.text:
1. Read the following EarSketch Curriculum sections and apply them to your song.

    • Section 8.1
    • Section 8.2
    • Section 8.3

  2. Write or modify a function to return something useful, such as the measure the function ends with.

  3. Modify the main program to use the return value from the function. For example, create a loop that calls your function multiple times and uses the return value from each call (such as the ending measure) to set the input to the next call (such as the starting measure).

  4. Allow a user (your DJ?) to customize your song by prompting them for input and using boolean logic to change the song.

docs.title: Grading Rubric
docs.text: Item Points At least one function returns a value. 40% The main program uses the function return value in a meaningful way. 40% The song is customizable with user input and boolean logic. 20%

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text:
Download your script from EarSketch and submit it:

  1. Click the toggle switch to expand the Content Manager.

  2. Select the SCRIPTS tab.

  3. Find your song's script in the MY SCRIPTS panel and click its Download button .

  4. Click the download button next to the Script option.

  5. Submit the downloaded Python (.py) file in Google Classroom.

  • Your song's script (.py file) submitted in Google Classroom.

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent A function returns a value the main program genuinely uses — an ending measure feeding the next section's start is the classic — and a listener can answer your prompt and hear the song change, with boolean logic steering it and both answers running clean. 3 — Above Average All three requirements met; the return value is used, but trivially — printed rather than steering anything. 2 — Average A function returns a value nobody uses, or the prompt crashes on one of the two answers. 1 — Below Average No return values and no working input — the conversation is still one-way. 0 — Failing Nothing submitted in Google Classroom.

docs.title: EarSketch: Release Day
docs.text: Every producer eventually has to ship. You've spent this unit learning tracks, beats, loops, effects, functions, and lists — now you'll put them into one final song and release it to your toughest audience: this class. We'll play every song on release day, and the class will vote for a winner. The stakes are bragging rights.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This is the culminating project for the EarSketch unit. You'll compose one complete, original song that shows off the skills from every lab, export it, and enter it in the class listening party.

You've got it when…

  • Your song is a complete piece with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
  • Someone reading your script can see every skill from the unit at work.
  • You'd play it for the class without apologizing first.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. This song is your work, start to finish.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: The point of a final project is to show what you can do. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Your Mission
docs.text:
1. Create a new script for your final song. You may reuse ideas — and your best sections — from the unit's labs.

  2. Compose a song at least 16 measures long that uses the skills from the unit. The grading rubric below is your feature checklist.

  3. Give your song a title. Every release needs one.

docs.title: The Listening Party
docs.text:
On release day, we'll play every song for the class. Each of you will vote for your top three songs, and you may not vote for your own. The song with the most votes wins the unit — and the accompanying bragging rights.

Info

The vote is a friendly competition, so keep it friendly: the class picks the winner, but the rubric decides your grade. An unpopular song that demonstrates every skill still earns full marks.

docs.title: Grading Rubric
docs.text: Item Points Complete song, at least 16 measures, with a clear beginning, middle, and end 20% At least four tracks, with a tempo you set 10% A beat you wrote with a beat string and makeBeat() 15% A for loop that repeats part of your song 10% At least two effects, at least one changed over time with an envelope 15% At least two custom functions with arguments that divide the song into sections 20% Your sounds organized in a list 10%

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text:
Download your final song from EarSketch and submit it — this time you'll turn in the audio along with the script, so we can play it on release day:

  1. Click the toggle switch to expand the Content Manager.

  2. Select the SCRIPTS tab.

  3. Find your final song's script in the MY SCRIPTS panel and click its Download button .

  4. In the download dialog, download both the Script option and the MP3 option.

  5. Submit both files in Google Classroom.

  • Your final song's script (.py file) submitted in Google Classroom.
  • Your final song's audio (.mp3 file) submitted in Google Classroom.

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent A complete, original song of at least 16 measures with a clear beginning, middle, and end, demonstrating every feature on the checklist — set tempo, your own beat string, a loop, effects with an envelope, argument-taking section functions, sounds in a list — with both the script and the MP3 submitted and ready to play at the party. 3 — Above Average A complete song with one feature missing or thin — an envelope that never changes, a list holding only some of the sounds. 2 — Average A song that plays but skips several checklist features, or runs short of 16 measures. 1 — Below Average Fragments of labs stitched together, or a script with no exported audio to play. 0 — Failing Nothing to play on release day.

docs.title: Toy Block
docs.text: This is a 2x4 toy block. Its manufacturer's lawyers would like everyone to call it exactly that, and we are happy to oblige. Today you'll model one in Autodesk Fusion, dimensionally accurate to the real thing, using the four tools that show up in 90% of all 3D designs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Nearly every model you will ever make in Fusion follows the same rhythm: draw a flat sketch, pull it into a 3D body, and refine it. In this lab you'll follow that rhythm four times over to build a toy block — base, studs, hollow underside, and rounded edges — and every dimension will match the brick in your junk drawer at home.

docs.title: The Tools You'll Meet
docs.text:
This lab introduces the core toolbox. Skim the tables now; each tool is explained again at the step where you first use it.

Modeling tools:

Tool What it does Where to find it Create Sketch Starts a 2D drawing on a flat plane or face Toolbar, or the Create menu 2-Point Rectangle Sketches a rectangle from two corners Sketch toolbar Center Diameter Circle Sketches a circle from its center Sketch toolbar, or C Line Sketches a line; doubles as a construction line in Construction mode Sketch toolbar; X toggles Construction Sketch Dimension Locks a size or distance with a number Sketch toolbar, or D Offset Sketch Copies sketch geometry a set distance from the original Sketch toolbar Extrude Pulls a 2D profile into a 3D body Solid toolbar, Create menu, or E Rectangular Pattern Repeats a feature in rows and columns Solid toolbar Shell Hollows out a solid body, leaving walls of a set thickness Modify ▸ Shell Fillet Rounds off a sharp edge Modify ▸ Fillet, or F

Interface features:

Feature What it's for Browser The design's table of contents: sketches, bodies, units, and visibility eyeballs Origin planes The three starting planes (XY, XZ, YZ) that align with the axes ViewCube and Home icon Spin the view to a standard angle; Home resets to the 3D perspective Parametric Timeline Records every feature you create, in order, and lets you edit any of them later Sketch Palette Sketch options like Construction and Look At Data Panel Your saved cloud files, organized into Projects and Folders

Before you start

Sign in to Autodesk Fusion with your Autodesk account. Your work saves to Autodesk's cloud, so you can pick it up from any computer in the lab.

You've got it when…

  • Your block measures 31.8 x 15.8 x 9.6 millimeters, with eight studs on top made from one extrude and one pattern.
  • The underside is hollowed to a 1.49 mm wall, with three columns down the center.
  • The stud, block, and column edges are rounded with a 0.2 mm fillet.
  • The design is saved to your Fusion project as 2x4 Toy Block.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. Ask a neighbor for a hand if you're stuck, but drive Fusion yourself.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: This lab is about learning the tools by using them, so set AI aside this time. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Start a Part Design
docs.text:
Every new Fusion file begins with a choice about what you're making.

  1. Open Fusion and create a new design. Fusion asks you to choose a design intent. Choose Part Design.

    The three design intents

    A Part Design is a single manufacturable object — like today's toy block. An Assembly Design combines multiple parts into a larger object, the way individual blocks build a structure. A Hybrid Design is the classic Fusion style, where one file can hold both. We'll start with parts and work up to assemblies later. You can change your mind later by converting the Design Type in the Browser.

  2. Reset Fusion to its default settings so your screen matches this lab. Click your profile icon, click Preferences, and click the Restore Defaults button in the lower left of the window.

    Tip

    If Restore Defaults is grayed out, you're already at the defaults and there's nothing to do.

  3. While still in Preferences, set the default units. On the left side, under Default Units, select Design and set the units to millimeter. Click Apply, then close the window.

    Default units vs. this file's units

    The Preference sets the unit for every new design file. Any single file can be changed at any time: in the Browser, open the Document Settings folder and click Change Active Units. Leave everything in millimeters for this unit — all of our dimensions are metric.

docs.title: Sketch the Base
docs.text:
Nearly all Fusion workflows start with a 2D sketch that you later pull into a 3D body. The block's footprint comes first.

  1. Click Create Sketch in the toolbar.

  2. Fusion asks you to pick one of the three origin planes. Select the bottom XY plane — picture it as the floor the block sits on. Fusion rotates your view to face the sketch straight on, and a Sketch tab appears in the toolbar.

    Why the straight-on view?

    Sketching in a straight-on view is an industry best practice. It removes perspective distortion, so dimensions land where you intend and your cursor doesn't snap to geometry hiding in the background.

  3. Select the 2-Point Rectangle tool.

  4. Click the origin point — the dot at the center of the screen — to place the rectangle's first corner.

    Why start at the origin?

    Starting at the origin anchors your design to a fixed point in space. An anchored sketch can't drift, and it's the first step toward a fully defined sketch — an idea we'll keep building on in the coming labs.

  5. Drag your mouse out and watch the two dimension inputs appear. Press Tab until the width input is active and type 15.8. Press Tab to lock it, type 31.8 for the length, and click in any quadrant to place the rectangle. For this block, the direction doesn't matter.

    Tip

    Typed a wrong number? Double-click any dimension to reopen it, type the new value, and press Enter.

  6. Look at your sketch lines. They changed from blue to black. In Fusion, black geometry is fully constrained — locked in place — while blue geometry can still move.

  7. Click Finish Sketch in the top right. This is your exit door back to the 3D world; Fusion needs to know you're done sketching before it hands you the 3D tools.

    Your model should look like this.

    The Browser is your table of contents

    A Sketches folder just appeared in the Browser on the left. The Browser lists everything in your design — sketches, bodies, and more — and the eyeball icons toggle visibility.

docs.title: Extrude the Base
docs.text:
1. Activate Extrude — press E, or find it in the Solid toolbar or the Create menu. The sketch has only one profile (an enclosed area a 3D tool can grab), so Fusion selects it for you.

  2. Type 9.6 for the distance. The value lands in the Extrude dialog — Fusion lets you type in the canvas or the dialog, whichever is handier.

  3. The flat, straight-on view is hiding the block's new thickness. Click the Home icon next to the ViewCube to switch to a 3D perspective.

  4. Before confirming, take a minute to practice moving around. You will do this hundreds of times per lab, so it's worth making it automatic.

    To do this Do this Zoom Roll the scroll wheel Pan Hold the scroll wheel down and move the mouse Orbit Hold Shift and the scroll wheel together, then move Reset the view Click the Home icon

  5. Click OK to confirm the extrude. A Bodies folder appears in the Browser.

    Your model should look like this.

    The Parametric Timeline is time travel

    Look at the bottom of the screen. The Parametric Timeline records every feature you create, in order. Double-click any item to edit it later — change this extrude's thickness next week and the rest of the model rebuilds to match. Right-click an item for more options, like Delete.

docs.title: Save Your Work
docs.text:
1. Click the Save icon in the Application bar at the top left.

    Where your files live

    Fusion stores files on Autodesk's servers, not on your computer. That's why you sign in — your designs follow your account to any machine.

  2. Name the design 2x4 Toy Block.

  3. Set up a home for this unit's work. Click the caret next to the Location field to expand the list, click New Project, and name it Fusion Labs. Save every design from this unit in this project.

  4. Add a folder inside the project: double-click the Fusion Labs project to open it, click New Folder, and name it Skill Labs.

    Warning

    This trips up nearly everyone: you must double-click the folder to open it before saving, or the file lands outside the folder. The location bar should show the folder's name before you commit.

  5. Click Save. The design tab now shows the file name and a version number — more on versioning later in the unit.

    Info

    The Data Panel, opened from the grid icon at the top left, shows all your saved files. You can also create projects and folders there and move files around.

docs.title: Add the First Stud
docs.text:
The eight studs on top start as a single circle. Pattern tools will do the other seven.

  1. Click Create Sketch, then click the top face of the block. With a 3D body in place, you can sketch directly on any of its flat faces.

  2. Select the Center Diameter Circle tool or press C. Click once anywhere on the top face to place the center — don't worry about the position yet — then type 5 for the diameter and click again to place the circle. Press Esc to end the command.

  3. The circle isn't pinned down yet — click and drag it and it slides around freely. Fusion uses constraints and sketch dimensions to lock geometry in place. Activate the Sketch Dimension tool or press D.

  4. Click the circle's center, then the top edge of the rectangle, and drag to the side. A dimension appears. Click again to place it, type 3.9, and press Enter.

    Info

    No need to type "mm" — you set millimeters as the default unit in step 3, and Fusion assumes it.

  5. Repeat in the other direction: dimension from the circle's center to the neighboring edge, also 3.9.

  6. Try to drag the circle again. It shouldn't budge — the two dimensions hold it in place.

    Your model should look like this.

  7. Press E for Extrude and select the circle's profile. This sketch has more than one profile, so Fusion waits for you to pick. Type 1.7 for the distance.

  8. Before clicking OK, check the Operation field: it should say Join. Keep it. Join fuses the new cylinder and the block into one body; New Body would leave a separate, disconnected cylinder resting on top. Click OK.

    Why Join matters here

    The Shell tool you'll use shortly traces the outside contour of a body. Because the stud is joined, Shell treats it as part of that contour — which is exactly what leaves the hollow indent inside each stud, just like the real block.

docs.title: Pattern the Studs
docs.text:
One stud down, seven to go. You could sketch seven more circles, but the Rectangular Pattern tool does it in one move — and if the stud ever changes, the copies follow.

  1. Activate Rectangular Pattern from the Solid toolbar.

    Pattern the feature, not the sketch

    Fusion also offers a sketch version of Rectangular Pattern. Avoid it. Patterning 3D features is far less taxing for Fusion than patterning sketch geometry, and simple sketches keep your model fast and easy to update. This is a best practice worth building early.

  2. Set the Object Type to Features, then select your stud extrude in the timeline at the bottom of the screen. The cylinder highlights blue when you have it.

  3. Click the Axes selector, then click the block's length edge first, followed by the width edge. Selecting the length first maps it to Axis 1 in the dialog, so your numbers will match the steps below.

  4. Drag the two directional arrows on the model to rough the pattern in. This visual check confirms the pattern heads across the block, not off into space, before you commit exact numbers.

  5. Set Axis 1 to a distance of 24 and a quantity of 4.

    Check the Distribution

    Make sure Distribution is set to Extent. Extent measures the total distance from the first stud to the last — not the gap between neighbors. If your preview scatters studs past the edge of the block, this setting is the usual suspect.

  6. Set Axis 2 to a quantity of 2 and an Extent distance of 8 for the second row.

    Tip

    If a pattern grows in the wrong direction, add or remove a minus sign on the distance.

  7. Click OK when the preview shows two tidy rows of four.

    Your model should look like this.

docs.title: Hollow the Bottom
docs.text:
1. Click and drag the ViewCube in the top right to turn the block over. The ViewCube snaps to standard views; dragging gives you anything in between.

  2. The block is still solid. Activate Shell from the Modify menu — you're modifying an existing body, which is how Fusion organizes its menus.

  3. Select only the bottom face, then set the Inside Thickness to 1.49. Click OK.

    Your model should look like this.

    Checkpoint

    Look inside each stud: the Shell traced the joined studs as part of the outer contour and left an indent inside every one. That's the Join from step 28 paying off.

docs.title: Add the Center Columns
docs.text:
A real 2x4 has three columns under the roof that grip the studs of the block below. They're built from one circle, an offset, and another pattern.

  1. Right-click the bottom inside face and choose Create Sketch — right-clicking a flat face is a second way to start a sketch. Check the Browser and turn off the visibility of your earlier sketches if they're in the way.

  2. Activate the Line tool, then turn on Construction in the Sketch Palette (or press X). A construction line draws dashed and is for reference only — it helps you line things up without adding a profile that Extrude would try to grab later.

  3. Hover over one of the recessed circles inside a stud until a circle glyph appears — that's Fusion offering to snap to the center. Click it, draw the line across the block to the center of the opposite circle, and click. Press Esc to end the Line command.

    Warning

    Snapping to existing geometry only works in a straight-on view. If your view has drifted, click Look At in the Sketch Palette to face the sketch directly.

  4. Press C for a circle, and turn Construction back off (press X). Hover along your construction line until the triangle glyph appears at its midpoint, click to place the center, and type 6.3 for the diameter.

  5. Now make the column hollow. Activate the Offset Sketch tool, select the circle, and type 1 for the offset distance. Use the Flip button until the new circle lands inside the original.

    Offset vs. Shell

    Offset is the other road to a hollow shape: it copies geometry a set distance away, giving you two profiles — a ring — to extrude directly. Shell hollows a finished body; Offset builds the hollow into the sketch. You'll use both, and today you're using each where it works best.

  6. Press E, select the ring profile between the two circles, and extrude 8.1. Click OK.

  7. Activate Rectangular Pattern again. It remembers the Features object type from last time. Select your newest extrude in the timeline, click the Axes selector, and select the block's long edge. Set the quantity to 3 and the distance to 16, then click OK.

    Your model should look like this.

docs.title: Fillet the Edges
docs.text:
The shape is done; the edges are not. Real blocks are molded with slightly rounded edges, and the fillet is the tool that rounds them.

  1. Activate Fillet from the Modify menu or press F.

    Pronunciation matters

    In CAD it's FILL-it, not fill-AY. The fish gets the French pronunciation; the edge does not.

  2. Take a minute to select every edge that needs rounding: the top edge of all eight studs, the outer edges of the block, and the base edges of the three bottom columns.

    Edges, not faces

    Click carefully on the edge, not the flat face beside it. Selecting a face fillets every edge attached to that face — which usually includes edges you didn't want.

  3. Set the fillet radius to 0.2 and click OK.

  4. Save your design — same Save icon as before. Fusion stores this as a new version of the same file.

    Your model should look like this.

Checkpoint

Base, studs, shell, columns, fillets — one block, five features, and every tool you'll lean on for the rest of this unit. Nice work.

Why 31.8 and not 32?

The numbers in this lab aren't random. The real brick lives on an 8-millimeter grid — a 2x4 spans 16 by 32 mm of grid — with 0.1 mm shaved from each side so neighboring blocks don't bind. That's how you get 31.8 x 15.8, and it's a taste of a design decision you'll make in your own parts: nominal size minus clearance.

docs.title: Challenges
docs.text:
Try these on your own once your block is done.

  • Time travel. Double-click the base extrude in the timeline and change 9.6 to 19.2. Watch the whole block — studs, shell, columns, and fillets — rebuild to double height. Change it back when you're done.
  • The 2x2. Model a 2x2 block from scratch, no instructions. Every dimension you need can be worked out from this lab and the 8 mm grid.
  • Reality check. Borrow the calipers, measure a real block, and compare it to your model's dimensions. Note what you find in your notebook.

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text:
• Your design saved as 2x4 Toy Block in the Fusion Labs project. It's on Autodesk's cloud, so saving is submitting — I can see it from the class hub.
  • A screenshot of your finished block pasted into your project notebook, with a sentence on which tool gave you the most trouble and why.

Credit: Adapted from Day 1 of Learn Autodesk Fusion in 30 Days (2026 Edition) by Kevin Kennedy, Product Design Online.

docs.title: First Python Program
docs.text: Every programmer's first program prints two words and does nothing useful. It's a tradition, and we're not going to break it. From there we'll add a couple of variables and a little math, and you'll have written and run real Python.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
We'll build this program together — I'll write it on the projector and talk through each line while you follow along on your own machine. Along the way you'll start the programming environment, create and save a Python script file, run it, and use variables with different data types.

How this one works

This is a follow-along lab. We write it as a class, one line at a time, on the projector. Keep pace, and stop me with questions — that's the point.

You've got it when…

  • Your program prints Hello, World!.
  • It prints your name and a fun fact about you.
  • It stores a number in a variable and prints it.
  • It prints the result of a calculation using that number.

Collaboration & AI

Work: Together as a class, then finish and save your own copy.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: This is your first program; type every line yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Your Program
docs.text:
Write a program that:

  • Prints Hello, World!.
  • Prints your name and a fun fact about yourself.
  • Stores your age (or another number, like a favorite number) in a variable and prints it.
  • Prints the result of a simple math operation with that number — for example, your age in five years, or double your favorite number.
  • Uses at least two different strings and one number.

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text: • Save the file as first_program.py and submit it.

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent first_program.py runs cleanly and prints all four required things — Hello, World!, your name and fun fact, your stored number, and a calculation — with the math done by Python from your variable, not typed in as an answer. At least two strings and one number, per the spec. 3 — Above Average Everything prints and the program runs, with a minor slip — a missing label on the calculation, or a number stored as a string. 2 — Average The program runs but skips a requirement — no variable, or no calculation, or the "math" is a number you typed yourself. 1 — Below Average The program doesn't run, or little beyond Hello, World! made it into the file. 0 — Failing Nothing submitted, or a file with no evidence you wrote a program.

docs.title: Turtle Power
docs.text:
Figure 1: Turtles in their natural habitat. This is real.

You're going to steer a turtle around the screen with code, leaving a trail behind it. First a maze, then a map of the neighborhood — with a very specific destination in mind.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Turtle graphics uses a "turtle" (a cursor) that moves around the screen, leaving a trail. By commanding it to move, turn, and change color, you can draw shapes, patterns, and whole pictures. In this lab you'll program the turtle to walk the solution to a maze, then to a map.

Before you start

The turtle library is built into Python — no install needed. Start a new program to use it.

You've got it when…

  • Your turtle walks from a starting triangle through the maze.
  • Your turtle travels from the NPA STEAM building to the Dutch Bros on the map.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. Ask a neighbor if you're stuck, but drive your own turtle.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Work out the turns and distances yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Introducing Turtle Graphics
docs.text:
To use the turtle library, we start by importing it.

import turtle

These commands are then available to make our graphic:

Command Description turtle.forward(distance) Move forward by distance, in the direction the turtle is headed. turtle.backward(distance) Move backward by distance, opposite the heading. turtle.goto(x, y) Move to a specific location. The origin (0, 0) is the center of the screen. turtle.home() Move to the origin (0, 0) and reset the heading. turtle.right(angle) Turn right by angle degrees. turtle.left(angle) Turn left by angle degrees. turtle.penup() Pick the pen up — no drawing while moving. turtle.pendown() Put the pen down — draw while moving. turtle.pensize(width) Change the thickness of the line. turtle.pencolor(colorstring) Set the pen color, e.g. "red", "yellow". turtle.bgcolor(color) Change the background color. turtle.circle(radius) Draw a circle with the given radius. turtle.dot(size, color) Draw a dot of the given size and color. turtle.clear() Erase everything in the graphics window. turtle.shape("turtle") Set the turtle's shape: "arrow", "turtle", "circle", "square", "triangle", or "classic".

docs.title: Turtle Maze
docs.text:
We'll program the turtle to walk the solution of a maze.

Download maze.gif

  1. Create a new file named maze.py with the following content.

    maze.py
    import turtle

turtle.shape("turtle")
turtle.bgpic("maze.gif")
turtle.penup()
turtle.goto(-70, 210)
turtle.pendown()
turtle.pencolor("red")

  2. Put maze.gif in the same folder as maze.py.

    Warning

    turtle.bgpic() only loads GIF images, and the file must sit in the same folder as your program or the turtle won't find it.

  3. Edit the goto arguments on line 6 to place the turtle at one of the maze's starting triangles. This takes some trial and error.

  4. Starting on line 9, add commands from the table above to guide the turtle through the maze.

docs.title: Turtle Map
docs.text:
Figure 2: Goals.

The maze was a lot of work, and our turtle could go for a Poppin' Boba Berry Lemonade from Dutch Bros.

Download map.gif

  1. Create a new file named map.py. Start from a copy of your maze.py.
  2. Put map.gif in the same folder as map.py, and change bgpic to load map.gif.
  3. Modify the program to guide the turtle from the NPA STEAM building (the blue dot) to the Dutch Bros.

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text:
• maze.py
  • map.py

You do not need to submit the image files.

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent Both programs work: in maze.py the turtle starts at a starting triangle and draws a path through the maze without cutting through walls, and in map.py it travels from the NPA STEAM building to the Dutch Bros. The routes are navigated with movement and turn commands, and the pen is down where the trail matters. 3 — Above Average Both programs run and reach their destinations, with a minor slip — a clipped corner, a grazed wall, or a trail that starts a step late. 2 — Average One of the two programs works, or the turtle "solves" the maze by jumping straight through walls to the exit. 1 — Below Average Neither program completes its route, or the turtle never leaves the start. 0 — Failing Nothing submitted, or no evidence the turtle ever moved.

docs.title: Turtle Spiral
docs.text: We're going to draw this spiral in NPA colors. Reading the directions, it looks like an enormous amount of typing — which is exactly the problem loops were invented to solve.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll draw a spiral, first by understanding the algorithm, then by teaching Python to repeat it with a while loop, tightening it into a for loop, and finally using if…else to switch colors partway through.

You've got it when…

  • Your spiral draws itself with a loop instead of hundreds of lines.
  • It runs 600 turns using a for loop and range().
  • It draws the first 300 turns in maroon and the rest in blue.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. Compare with a neighbor, but write your own loop.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Loops are the whole point here; reason them out yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Spiraling Into Madness
docs.text:
Start with this code.

import turtle
turtle.bgcolor("black")
turtle.speed(15)

Here's the algorithm to draw the spiral:

  1. Set the pen color to "maroon".
  2. Walk in a pattern:
    1. Walk forward 1 step.
    2. Turn right 121 degrees.
    3. Walk forward 2 steps.
    4. Turn right 121 degrees.
    5. Walk forward 3 steps.
    6. Turn right 121 degrees.
    7. …and so on.
  3. Repeat this pattern, increasing the number of steps by one each move, 300 times.
  4. Change the pen color to "blue" and continue the pattern 300 more times.

Simple, right? Here are the commands you'll need:

Command Description turtle.forward(distance) Move forward by distance. turtle.right(angle) Turn right by angle degrees. turtle.pencolor(colorstring) Set the pen color. turtle.bgcolor(color) Set the background color.

docs.title: While Loop
docs.text:
Writing out hundreds of lines is painful for humans. Computers are great at doing the same thing over and over. Notice the two commands that repeat in the algorithm: walk forward and turn right. We can write them once and tell Python to loop them.

Read the syntax for a while loop, then loop the two turtle commands 600 times to draw the spiral in a single color.

Checkpoint

Submit a copy of your program (.py) at this point.

docs.title: For Loop
docs.text:
In the while loop, you used a counter variable, i, to track how many times the loop ran and how many steps to take. Counting loop iterations is so common that Python has a loop just for it: the for loop.

Read the syntax for a for loop, focusing on the range() function, then rewrite your program to use a for loop instead of a while loop.

Checkpoint

Submit a copy of your program (.py) at this point.

docs.title: If…Else
docs.text:
We're almost done, but we need to switch the pen color from maroon to blue when we're 300 turns into the 600-turn loop. The program has to make a decision based on a condition — called selection.

Read the syntax for conditionals and if…else, then add code inside your loop to do this:

  • If the loop has run fewer than 300 times, set the pen color to "maroon".
  • Else set the pen color to "blue".

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text: • Your finished spiral program (.py).

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent Your finished program draws the full 600-turn spiral with a for loop and range(), switches from maroon to blue at turn 300 with an if…else inside the loop, and both checkpoint versions (while, then for) were submitted along the way — the progression is visible, not just the destination. 3 — Above Average The finished spiral draws correctly, with a minor slip — a checkpoint missed, the colors swapped, or the switch a turn or two off. 2 — Average A loop draws the spiral but there's no color switch, or only the while-loop version works. 1 — Below Average No working loop — the turtle draws a few segments and stops, or the program doesn't run. 0 — Failing Nothing submitted, or hundreds of pasted forward/right lines and no loop in sight.

docs.title: Grade Calculator
docs.text: So far your programs have done all the talking. Now we'll let the user talk back. You'll ask for a number of points and hand back a letter grade — which means reading input, turning text into a number, and making a decision.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll learn to get input from the user, cast that text into a number, and write a function that uses conditionals to turn points into a letter grade.

You've got it when…

  • Your program asks the user for a number of points.
  • A calculate_grade() function returns the correct letter grade.
  • The program prints the letter grade to the screen.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. A neighbor can help you debug; the logic is yours.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Write the conditionals yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Getting Input From the User
docs.text:
input() is a built-in function that pauses your program and waits for the user to type something.

  • Whatever the user types comes back as a string (text), even if they type numbers.
  • The program continues once the user presses Enter.
name = input("What is your name?")
print("Hello, " + name)

How it works:

  1. Python shows the prompt: What is your name?
  2. The user types something (say, Steve) and presses Enter.
  3. The string "Steve" is stored in the variable name.

docs.title: Casting
docs.text:
input() always returns a string. To use what the user typed as a number, first cast it:

  • int() — makes an integer (whole number) from a string.
  • float() — makes a floating-point (decimal) number from a string.

After working with a number, you may need to cast back to a string to concatenate it (+) with other text for printing:

  • str() — makes a string from a number.
age_string = input("What is your age?")
age = int(age_string)
print("In ten years, you will be " + str(age + 10) + " years old.")

The first two lines can be combined by passing input() straight into int():

age = int(input("What is your age?"))

docs.title: Grade Calculator
docs.text:
Design a program that calculates a letter grade using this scale:

Points Grade 90 to 100 A 80 to <90 B 70 to <80 C 60 to <70 D <60 F

Do this:

  1. Write a function with this signature: calculate_grade(points).
  2. The function expects an integer number of points (the points argument).
  3. Use conditionals (if, elif, and else) with the table above to determine the grade.
  4. The function returns the correct letter grade.
  5. This function does not use print().
  6. Write a main program that asks the user for a number of points with input(), calls your calculate_grade() function, and prints the letter grade it returns.

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text: • Your Python (.py) file with the grade-calculation program.

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent calculate_grade(points) returns the right letter for every band — including the boundaries 90, 80, 70, and 60 — and never prints. The main program gets the points with input(), casts them, calls your function, and prints what comes back. You tested the edges, not just one number from the middle. 3 — Above Average The program works end to end, with a minor slip — one boundary off by a point, or a stray print left inside the function. 2 — Average Grades come out wrong for several bands, the function prints instead of returning, or the conditional logic lives in the main program with no function. 1 — Below Average The program doesn't run, or there's no conditional logic to grade with. 0 — Failing Nothing submitted, or no evidence of the calculator.

docs.title: Guess the Number
docs.text: You'll build a game where the player hunts for a secret random number. The trick is to keep the main program short and readable by pushing the fiddly details — getting valid input, checking the guess — into their own functions.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll write three helper functions and a main program that ties them together into a working guessing game.

You've got it when…

  • get_range() asks the user for the top of the range and rejects bad input.
  • get_guess(top) asks for a guess and rejects out-of-range input.
  • check_guess(guess, secret) returns True or False.
  • The game loops until the player guesses the secret number.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. Compare approaches with a neighbor, but write your own functions.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Design the functions and the loop yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Create a get_range Function
docs.text:
This function sets up the game by asking the user for the range of numbers to guess from. Name it get_range with this behavior:

  1. get_range() accepts no arguments.
  2. Ask the user for a maximum number to guess. (To guess between 1 and 100, the user enters 100.)
  3. Cast the user's entry to an int.
  4. Store the int in a variable called top.
  5. Don't allow an illegal number — loop steps 2–3 while the number entered is less than 1.
  6. Return top.

docs.title: Create a get_guess Function
docs.text:
This function asks the user to guess a number. Name it get_guess:

  1. get_guess(top) accepts one argument: the maximum number in the range.
  2. Ask the user to guess a number between 1 and top.
  3. Cast the entry to an int.
  4. Store the int in a variable called guess.
  5. Don't allow an illegal number — loop steps 2–3 while the number is less than 1 or greater than top.
  6. Return guess.

docs.title: Create a check_guess Function
docs.text:
Name this function check_guess:

  1. check_guess(guess, secret) accepts two arguments: a guessed number and the secret number.
  2. Check whether guess equals secret. Return True if it does, False if it doesn't.

docs.title: The Main Program
docs.text:
Python's random module makes random selections. We'll use it for the secret number. Put this at the top of your file:

import random

Get a random integer between 1 and 10 like this:

secret_number = random.randint(1, 10)

Now write the main program:

  1. Say Welcome to Guess the Number!
  2. Call get_range() and store its result.
  3. Call random.randint() to get a secret number in the range the user asked for (pass it 1 and the result of step 2). Store it.
  4. Call get_guess() and store its result.
  5. Call check_guess(), passing it the secret number (step 3) and the guess (step 4).
  6. If check_guess() returned False, say Nope!
  7. Loop steps 4, 5, and 6 until check_guess() returns True.
  8. Print You guessed correctly!

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text: • Your Python (.py) file.

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent All three functions match their specs — get_range() and get_guess(top) loop until they get a legal number, check_guess(guess, secret) returns True or False — and the main program picks its secret with random.randint, loops until the guess lands, and says so. Bad input can't break the game; you tried. 3 — Above Average The game plays start to finish, with a slip — one validation hole (say, a 0 sneaks through), or a function that works but strays from its spec. 2 — Average The game only works when the player behaves — validation missing — or one of the three functions is absent, with its job inlined into the main program. 1 — Below Average The game can't be played to a win, or the program doesn't run. 0 — Failing Nothing submitted, or no evidence of the game.

docs.title: Slot Machine
docs.text: A slot machine is just a random pick from a set of symbols, three times in a row. You already know random; now you'll store the symbols in a list and pull from it.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll build a Python list of symbols and write a slot function that prints three random symbols from it — a one-line jackpot generator.

You've got it when…

  • You have a list holding each of the slot symbols.
  • random.choice() pulls a random symbol from the list.
  • Your slot function prints three random symbols.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. A neighbor can help, but write your own function.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Build the list and loop yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Create a List of Strings
docs.text:
Create a Python list of strings, with one string for each of these symbols:

🍒 🍋 🍊 🍉 🔔 💎 💲 🍀

Tip

Use the copy button on the block above to grab the symbols, then split them into separate strings in your list.

docs.title: Random Selection
docs.text:
We used the random library before to pick random numbers with randint. Now we'll use another function from random named choice to pick a random item from a list.

Put this at the top of your file:

import random

Use it like this, where mylist is the name of your list variable:

item = random.choice(mylist)

Try writing code to print a random item from the list in the section above.

docs.title: A Slot Machine
docs.text:
Write a function named slot:

  1. slot accepts a single argument: a list of symbol strings to choose from.
  2. Use a for loop with range() to repeat this three times:
    1. Make a random selection from the list.
    2. print the selected symbol to the screen.

Write a main program that creates the list from the first section, then passes it to your slot function.

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text: • Your Python (.py) file.

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent Your list holds all eight symbols, slot takes the list as its argument and uses a for loop with range() to print three random.choice picks, and the main program builds the list and passes it in — the function works from what it's given, not from a global it happens to see. 3 — Above Average The machine spins correctly, with a minor slip — a symbol or two missing from the list, or an extra print cluttering the output. 2 — Average Three random symbols appear, but by copy-paste instead of a loop, or without a slot function taking the list. 1 — Below Average The list exists but little else runs. 0 — Failing Nothing submitted, or no evidence of the machine.

docs.title: Dice Roller and Turtle Spirals Revisited
docs.text: Three short programs that lean on lists and one very useful operator. You'll roll dice, then come back to the spiral and color it two new ways — one random, one that marches through a list in order.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll write a dice-rolling function, then revisit the spiral to pick colors from a list — first randomly, then sequentially using the modulus operator.

You've got it when…

  • roll_dice(sides) returns a random number from 1 to sides.
  • Your random_spiral.py picks a random color for each move.
  • Your sequential_spiral.py steps through the color list in order, repeating.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. Compare with a neighbor, but write your own code.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: The modulus trick is the lesson; work it out yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Rolling Dice
docs.text:
1. Create a new Python file, dice.py.
  2. Write a function roll_dice(sides) that returns a random number between 1 and sides.
  3. Write a main program that calls roll_dice with different inputs. For example:
    • Roll a 6-sided die: roll_dice(6)
    • Roll a 20-sided die: roll_dice(20)

docs.title: Turtle Spiral Revisited
docs.text:
Here is the basic code for the two-colored spiral you made before.

import turtle
turtle.bgcolor("black")
turtle.speed(15)

for i in range(600):
    if i < 300:
        turtle.pencolor("maroon")
    else:
        turtle.pencolor("blue")
    turtle.forward(i)
    turtle.right(121)

Copy this code to a new file, random_spiral.py. Modify it to choose a random color from the list below for each turtle move, instead of switching between just two colors.

These are some of the color strings Python knows:

colors = ["red", "blue", "green", "yellow", "orange", "purple",
          "pink", "brown", "black", "white", "gray"]

docs.title: Sequential Spiral Colors
docs.text:
Copy your Section 2 code to a new file, sequential_spiral.py. Modify it to select colors from the list sequentially rather than randomly.

Hints

  • Recall list indexes (see Loop Through the Index Numbers on this page).
  • Consider the modulus operator (see this page, and try it).
  • Get the length of a list with len.
  • Think about using the modulus operator with the loop index i and the list length to walk the colors in order, over and over.

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text:
• dice.py
  • random_spiral.py
  • sequential_spiral.py

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent All three files work: roll_dice(sides) returns 1 through sides for any die you hand it, random_spiral.py picks a fresh random color every move, and sequential_spiral.py walks the color list in order and wraps around using the modulus operator with the loop index and len() — the trick, visible in one line. 3 — Above Average All three run, with a slip — a die that can roll 0, or a sequential spiral that cycles correctly but hard-codes the list length. 2 — Average Two of the three programs work, or the "sequential" spiral is secretly random or still two-colored. 1 — Below Average One program works, or none run. 0 — Failing Nothing submitted, or no evidence of the three programs.

docs.title: Rock Paper Scissors
docs.text: Time to put it together: input, functions, conditionals, and loops in one small game against the computer. Get the basic version working first, then make it friendlier to play.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll build a text-based Rock, Paper, Scissors game with three functions and a main program, then improve it with repeated play and more forgiving input.

You've got it when…

  • The computer makes a random choice and the player is prompted for theirs.
  • The game correctly reports a win, loss, or tie.
  • (Improved) The game repeats until the player quits, and accepts any capitalization or a single letter.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. A neighbor can help you debug; the logic is yours.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Write the game logic yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Create these functions:

  • get_computer_choice() — accepts no arguments; returns one of rock, paper, or scissors at random.
  • get_player_choice() — accepts no arguments; prompts the user to choose rock, paper, or scissors and returns the chosen string. It rejects any illegal string and keeps prompting until a valid one is entered.
  • determine_winner(player, computer) — accepts two strings, each expected to be rock, paper, or scissors. It compares them and prints one of:
    • You win! if the player won
    • I win! if the computer won
    • Tie! if the choices match

Rules:

  • Rock beats Scissors
  • Scissors beat Paper
  • Paper beats Rock
  • Matching choices tie

docs.title: Main Program
docs.text:
Write a main program that:

  1. Calls get_player_choice() and stores the player's choice.
  2. Calls get_computer_choice() and stores the computer's choice.
  3. Prints what the computer chose: I chose ____.
  4. Calls determine_winner(), passing it the player's and computer's choices.

docs.title: Improvements
docs.text:
Warning

Do not begin this section until Section 3 is working properly.

docs.title: Repeated Gameplay
docs.text:
1. Enclose the main program in an infinite while loop so the game plays over and over.
  2. Modify get_player_choice() to allow a fourth option: quit.
  3. Modify the main program to break out of the loop and quit if the player chooses quit.

docs.title: Simplified User Input
docs.text:
1. Modify get_player_choice() to accept any capitalization by modifying the string the user types to all lowercase. Only lowercase strings may be returned. (rock, Rock, ROCK, and RoCk should all return rock.)

  2. Modify get_player_choice() to accept a single letter for each choice (r, p, s, q). The function must still return the full word. The player may type the full word or just the letter.

    See the startswith string function for one way to do this.

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text: • Your Python (.py) file.

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent The full game with both improvements: all nine choice combinations report the right winner (and ties tie), play repeats until quit, and get_player_choice() takes any capitalization or a single letter but only ever returns the lowercase word. You checked all nine combos, not just the three you like throwing. 3 — Above Average The improved game works, with a slip — one combo reported wrong, or one input form (say, RoCk) slipping past the cleanup. 2 — Average The base game plays one round correctly but the improvements are missing, or the winner logic is wrong in several combinations. 1 — Below Average The game can't finish a round, or the program doesn't run. 0 — Failing Nothing submitted, or no evidence of the game.

docs.title: Getting Set Up for Pygame Zero
docs.text: Over the next several labs you'll build real video games: an alien dodging a bee, tanks that hunt you down, weights falling from the sky, and an infinite runner with costumes and a Game Over screen. Every game studio starts somewhere. Ours starts with a folder named images.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In this lab you'll install the Pygame Zero library in Thonny, make a home folder for your games, download every image the whole unit needs in one zip file, and run a tiny test program to prove your setup works. Ten minutes here saves a headache in every lab that follows.

Before you start

Open Thonny. If you can't find it on your computer, ask for help before continuing.

You've got it when…

  • pgzero shows as installed in Thonny's package manager.
  • You have a Pygame Zero folder with a folder named images inside it.
  • The images folder holds all 41 game images from the download.
  • Your test program opens a window with the alien on a sky-blue background.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. Ask a neighbor for a hand if you're stuck, but do the setup on your own computer.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: This lab is about learning where your files live, and only you know where you put them. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Install Pygame Zero
docs.text:
Thonny comes with Python built in, but the Pygame Zero library is a separate piece. Thonny has a package manager for exactly this job, so there's nothing to download from a website.

  1. In Thonny, open the menu Tools ▸ Manage packages…

  2. Type pgzero into the search box at the top and click Search on PyPI.

  3. Click pgzero in the search results, then click Install. When the progress messages stop, click Close.

Warning

The package is named exactly pgzero — no spaces, and no "pygame" in front. Similarly named packages are not the library we want.

Info

If pgzero already appears in the list of installed packages when the window opens, someone has beaten you to it. Skip to the next section.

docs.title: Make a Home for Your Games
docs.text:
Every game you write in this unit will live in one folder, next to one shared images folder. Keeping them together is not just tidiness — Pygame Zero only looks for images in a folder named images sitting beside your program.

  1. In your Documents folder (or wherever your teacher tells you), create a new folder named pygame-zero.

docs.title: Download the Game Images
docs.text:
Your games will star an alien, a bee, two tanks, some hearts, and a small wardrobe of runner costumes. All 41 images are in one zip file.

  1. Download the zip file.

    Download pygame-zero-images.zip

  2. Double-click the downloaded file to unpack it. On Windows, right-click it and choose Extract All… instead. Either way, you end up with a folder named images.

  3. Move the images folder into your pygame-zero folder.

Warning

The folder must be named exactly images — all lowercase, no spaces — and it must sit inside your pygame-zero folder, next to the programs you'll write. Pygame Zero will not look anywhere else.

What's in the zip?

All 41 images for the whole unit, so you only do this download once. Each lab also offers its own images as individual downloads, in case one ever goes missing.

docs.title: Test Your Setup
docs.text:
The smallest possible game will tell us whether everything is in the right place.

  1. In Thonny, create a new program and save it as alien_test.py in your pygame-zero folder — next to the images folder, not inside it.

  2. Type this program.

    alien_test.py
    import pgzrun

WIDTH = 800
HEIGHT = 600

alien = Actor("alien")
alien.x = WIDTH / 2
alien.y = HEIGHT / 2

def draw():
    screen.fill("skyblue")
    alien.draw()

pgzrun.go()

  3. Run your program with the Run button (or press F5). Your screen should look like this.

The bookends

Two lines in that program do jobs our old editor used to do for us. import pgzrun is the first line of every game — it loads the Pygame Zero library. pgzrun.go() is the last line — it starts the game running. Everything between the bookends is your game. Every program in this unit begins and ends exactly this way.

Where did the alien come from?

Actor("alien") found alien.png in your images folder by name — no .png needed. That's the whole reason the folder matters.

Checkpoint

If the alien is on your screen, your setup is done and every lab in this unit will find its images. If you got an error instead, check that alien_test.py sits next to (not inside) the images folder, and that the folder name is exactly images. An error like No module named 'pgzrun' means the library isn't installed — go back to Install Pygame Zero at the top of this lab.

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text: • Submit your alien_test.py file in Google Classroom.

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent Your alien_test.py runs as-is: a window opens with the alien centered on sky blue. That only happens when everything upstream is right — pgzero installed, all 41 images inside a folder named exactly images, and your program saved next to that folder, not inside it. 3 — Above Average The setup works with a minor slip you had to fix along the way — the file saved in the wrong spot and moved, or a mistyped folder name corrected at the checkpoint. 2 — Average pgzero is installed and the folders exist, but the test program errors or was never finished. 1 — Below Average Little of the setup done — no images folder in place, or no test program at all. 0 — Failing Nothing submitted, or no evidence of the setup.

docs.title: Multiple Worlds and Game Over Reset
docs.text: This is the big one: an infinite runner with a character-select screen, a running score, a Game Over screen, and a reset that puts everything back for the next round. The secret to keeping all of that manageable isn't more code — it's smaller functions.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In this lab you'll build an infinite runner and organize it into modes — costume, play, and game over — each with its own drawing and behavior. Along the way you'll animate a running character from a list of images, spawn obstacles on a timer, and write a reset() function that restarts the game cleanly.

Builds on: Tiled Images, Animated Motion, and Health — helper functions, lists of Actors, and collidelist().

Before you start

Open Thonny and start a new program named runner.py. Save it in your pygame-zero folder, next to your images folder.

You've got it when…

  • The game opens on a costume screen where Space changes characters and Enter starts the game.
  • The runner animates, jumps with Space, and dodges cacti that arrive on a timer.
  • Hitting an obstacle shows Game Over with the final score still visible.
  • Pressing Enter from Game Over resets everything and returns to the costume screen.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. Ask a neighbor for a hand if you're stuck, but the program you submit should be yours.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: The whole point of this lab is learning to organize a bigger program yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: New Images
docs.text:
This lab requires a lot of new images — three full costumes plus a cactus. If you completed Getting Set Up for Pygame Zero, they are already in your images folder and you can skip these steps.

  1. Download the zip file of images.

    Download runner-images.zip

  2. Double-click the zip file to open it. It will create a new folder next to the zip file with the same name.

  3. Move the images from the new folder into your game's images folder.

docs.title: Overview of the Game
docs.text: We're going to make an infinite runner type game. Dino Jump is an example of this type of game.

docs.title: Making Functions
docs.text:
We're going to focus on breaking up our code into a number of small functions to organize our game. This will help us add new behaviors, such as showing different screens for selecting a character and resetting the game after a Game Over screen is shown.

  1. Let's start a new game with the code below.

    runner.py
    import pgzrun

WIDTH = 800
HEIGHT = 600

runner = Actor("ninja0")
runner.x = 100
runner.y = 400

def draw():
    screen.fill("skyblue")
    screen.draw.filled_rect(Rect(0, 400,800, 200), (88, 242, 152))
    runner.draw()

pgzrun.go()

    Try your program. Your screen should look like this.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
When we're done, we want our game to have three modes:

  • costume — this mode will show a start screen where the player can choose a character.
  • play — this mode will show the game itself.
  • game over — this mode will show a Game Over screen with an option to reset.

We'll need to keep track of which mode we're currently in, to know how to update and what to draw. Let's create a variable for this.

  1. Add the highlighted line. We'll call the normal game mode play.

    runner = Actor("ninja0")
runner.x = 100
runner.y = 400
runner.mode = "play"

  2. Now let's take the code from our draw() function and put it in a helper function that will be used to draw the game when in play mode. We'll name this function draw_game().

    def draw_game():
    screen.fill("skyblue")
    screen.draw.filled_rect(Rect(0, 400,800, 200), (88, 242, 152))
    runner.draw()

  3. Finally, we need to call our draw_game() function from the draw() function, but only if we are in play mode. Replace the code in the draw() function so it looks like this.

    def draw():
    if runner.mode == "play":
        draw_game()

    Try your program. Your screen should look like it did before.

docs.title: Animation
docs.text:
Let's add a list of images to animate the character running. We'll also need to keep track of which image is currently shown, so we know which to move to on the next frame.

  1. Add the highlighted lines.

    runner = Actor("ninja0")
runner.x = 100
runner.y = 400
runner.mode = "play"
runner.images = ["ninja0", "ninja1", "ninja2", "ninja3", "ninja4", "ninja5",
                 "ninja6", "ninja7", "ninja8", "ninja9"]
runner.img_num = 0

  2. Add this function to change to the next image in the list.

    def next_runner_image():
    runner.image = runner.images[runner.img_num % len(runner.images)]
    runner.img_num += 1

    Something new!

    Instead of writing out the line to add one like this:

    runner.img_num = runner.img_num + 1

    we'll use this shorter version:

    runner.img_num += 1

    These two lines do exactly the same thing! The += operator is built into Python because we do addition so often as programmers. You can also subtract one like this:

    runner.img_num -= 1

  3. Call the next_runner_image() function from the update() function.

    def update():
    next_runner_image()

    Try your program. Your character should be animated to move like it is running.

docs.title: Keyboard Input
docs.text:
Now we'll make the character jump when Space is pressed. We'll use the built-in on_key_down() function to capture key presses.

  1. Define variables for the level of the ground and gravity. Add the highlighted lines.

    import pgzrun

WIDTH = 800
HEIGHT = 600
GROUND = 400
GRAVITY = 1

  2. Define a variable on the runner to keep track of vertical speed. Add the highlighted line.

    runner = Actor("ninja0")
runner.x = 100
runner.y = 400
runner.mode = "play"
runner.images = ["ninja0", "ninja1", "ninja2", "ninja3", "ninja4", "ninja5",
                 "ninja6", "ninja7", "ninja8", "ninja9"]
runner.img_num = 0
runner.speed_y = 0

  3. Add the built-in on_key_down() function to listen for key presses. We only want to jump if we're in play mode.

    def on_key_down(key):
    if runner.mode == "play":
        if key == keys.SPACE and runner.y == GROUND:
            runner.speed_y = -15

  4. Add a helper function to handle gravity.

    def apply_gravity():
    runner.y += runner.speed_y
    runner.speed_y += GRAVITY
    if runner.y > GROUND:
        runner.speed_y = 0
        runner.y = GROUND

  5. Finally, call the apply_gravity() function from the update() function, but only if we're in play mode. Add the highlighted lines.

    def update():
    next_runner_image()

    if runner.mode == "play":
        apply_gravity()

    Try your program. The character should jump when Space is pressed, then fall back to the ground.

docs.title: Obstacles
docs.text:
Next we'll add obstacles to jump over, and a timeout to keep track of how often new obstacles appear on the screen.

  1. Add the highlighted lines to create a list to hold obstacles and a timeout.

    runner = Actor("ninja0")
runner.x = 100
runner.y = 400
runner.mode = "play"
runner.images = ["ninja0", "ninja1", "ninja2", "ninja3", "ninja4", "ninja5",
                 "ninja6", "ninja7", "ninja8", "ninja9"]
runner.img_num = 0
runner.speed_y = 0
runner.obstacles_timeout = 0

obstacles = []

  2. Create a helper function to handle creating obstacles and moving them from right to left on the screen.

    def do_obstacles():
    # obstacles
    runner.obstacles_timeout += 1
    if runner.obstacles_timeout > 50:
        c = Actor('cactus')
        c.x = 850
        c.y = 430
        obstacles.append(c)
        runner.obstacles_timeout = 0

    for o in obstacles.copy():
        o.x -= 8
        if o.x < 0:
            obstacles.remove(o)

  3. Call the helper function from the update() function. It should only be called when we're in play mode. Add the highlighted line.

    def update():
    next_runner_image()
    if runner.mode == "play":
        apply_gravity()
        do_obstacles()

  4. Finally, add code to draw each obstacle in our drawing helper function. Add the highlighted lines.

    def draw_game():
    screen.fill("skyblue")
    screen.draw.filled_rect(Rect(0, 400,800, 200), (88, 242, 152))
    runner.draw()
    for o in obstacles:
        o.draw()

    Try your program. You should see obstacles appear at the timeout interval and move across the screen.

docs.title: Score
docs.text:
We'll keep score by counting each frame. The longer the player goes without hitting an obstacle, the higher the score.

  1. Create a variable to keep track of the score, starting from zero. Add the highlighted line.

    runner = Actor("ninja0")
runner.x = 100
runner.y = 400
runner.mode = "play"
runner.images = ["ninja0", "ninja1", "ninja2", "ninja3", "ninja4", "ninja5",
                 "ninja6", "ninja7", "ninja8", "ninja9"]
runner.img_num = 0
runner.speed_y = 0
runner.obstacles_timeout = 0
runner.score = 0

  2. Add one to the score in the update() function for each frame, but only if we're in the play mode. Add the highlighted line.

    def update():
    next_runner_image()
    if runner.mode == "play":
        apply_gravity()
        do_obstacles()
        runner.score += 1

  3. Add a helper function to draw the score on the screen.

    def draw_score():
    screen.draw.text(f"Score: {runner.score}", (30, 30), color="white", fontsize=60)

  4. Finally, call the helper function from the draw() function. Add the highlighted line.

    def draw():
    if runner.mode == "play":
        draw_game()
        draw_score()

    Try your program. The score should be constantly increasing, shown in the upper-left corner.

docs.title: Game Over and Reset
docs.text:
When the character touches an obstacle, the game ends. We want to show a Game Over screen and provide an option to reset and start a new game.

When the game ends, we'll move from the play mode to the game over mode.

  1. Create a helper function to check if the character has collided with an obstacle. If so, change the mode to game over.

    def check_damage():
    if runner.collidelist(obstacles) >= 0:
        runner.mode = "game over"

  2. Call the helper function from the update() function. Add the highlighted line.

    def update():
    next_runner_image()
    if runner.mode == "play":
        apply_gravity()
        do_obstacles()
        runner.score += 1
        check_damage()

  3. Create a helper function to draw the screen when we're in the game over mode.

    def draw_game_over():
    screen.fill("black")
    screen.draw.text("GAME OVER", center=(WIDTH / 2, HEIGHT / 2),
                     color="white", fontsize=60)
    screen.draw.text("Press Return to restart", center=(WIDTH / 2, HEIGHT / 2 + 50),
                     color="white", fontsize=60)

  4. Call the helper function from the draw() function when we're in the game over mode. Add the highlighted lines.

    def draw():
    if runner.mode == "play":
        draw_game()
        draw_score()
    elif runner.mode == "game over":
        draw_game_over()

    Try your program. You should see the Game Over screen when the player collides with an obstacle.

    The game ends correctly, but we'd like to show the final score. This is why we wrapped the score-drawing code up in its own function — now we can call it from multiple modes (play and game over) without repeating code.

  5. Add the highlighted line.

    def draw():
    if runner.mode == "play":
        draw_game()
        draw_score()
    elif runner.mode == "game over":
        draw_game_over()
        draw_score()

    Try your program. Now the final score should remain visible on the Game Over screen.

Now we need to add the code to restart the game when the player presses the Return key in game over mode. Let's create a function that "puts everything back" to the way it should be when a new game starts. This function will:

  • Set the score back to zero.
  • Set the runner's vertical speed back to zero.
  • Clear the list of obstacles, and reset the timeout for new obstacles to appear.
  • Change the mode from game over back to play.

  1. Add the function below to your program.

    def reset():
    runner.score = 0
    runner.speed_y = 0
    obstacles.clear()
    runner.obstacles_timeout = 0
    runner.mode = "play"

  2. Next, let's call this helper function when Enter is pressed, but only if we're in the game over mode. Add the highlighted lines.

    def on_key_down(key):
    if runner.mode == "play":
        if key == keys.SPACE and runner.y == GROUND:
            runner.speed_y = -15
    elif runner.mode == "game over":
        if key == keys.RETURN:
            reset()

    Try your program. You should be able to start a new game from the Game Over screen by pressing Enter.

docs.title: Changing Characters
docs.text:
That was a lot of work! But now we have a structure that lets us make other large modifications easily, such as adding additional modes. Let's add a mode for a screen that appears before the game starts, where the player chooses a costume.

Important concept

We're not going to create different Actors. We'll keep our single Actor named runner, but let the player choose which list of images that Actor wears. That's why we call the new mode costume — we're really just picking a costume for our Actor!

  1. First, set the starting mode for our program to the new one we'll create now. Make the highlighted update, changing the first mode from play to costume.

    runner = Actor("ninja0")
runner.x = 100
runner.y = 400
runner.mode = "costume"
runner.images = ["ninja0", "ninja1", "ninja2", "ninja3", "ninja4", "ninja5",
                 "ninja6", "ninja7", "ninja8", "ninja9"]
runner.img_num = 0
runner.speed_y = 0
runner.obstacles_timeout = 0
runner.score = 0

  2. Next, we'll create a new helper function to draw the costume screen. Add this to your code.

    def draw_costume():
    screen.fill("black")
    runner.draw()
    screen.draw.text("Press Space to select a player",
                     centerx=WIDTH / 2, top=20, color="white", fontsize=60)
    screen.draw.text("Press Return to start",
                     center=(WIDTH / 2, HEIGHT / 2), color="white", fontsize=60)

  3. Now update the draw() function to call the helper function when we're in costume mode. Add the highlighted lines.

    def draw():
    if runner.mode == "play":
        draw_game()
        draw_score()
    elif runner.mode == "game over":
        draw_game_over()
        draw_score()
    elif runner.mode == "costume":
        draw_costume()

    Try your program. It should draw the costume screen to start, now.

  4. Let's write a helper function to change to the next costume based on the costume we're currently wearing. We'll use the startswith() function, which is built into Python, to see what the Actor's current image name starts with. Add this to your code.

    def change_costume():
    if runner.image.startswith("ninja"):
        runner.images = ["dino0", "dino1", "dino2", "dino3", "dino4", "dino5",
                         "dino6", "dino7"]
    elif runner.image.startswith("dino"):
        runner.images = ["knight0", "knight1", "knight2", "knight3", "knight4",
                         "knight5", "knight6", "knight7", "knight8", "knight9"]
    elif runner.image.startswith("knight"):
        runner.images = ["ninja0", "ninja1", "ninja2", "ninja3", "ninja4", "ninja5",
                         "ninja6", "ninja7", "ninja8", "ninja9"]

  5. Finally, we'll handle the keyboard keys for the new costume mode. We'll call the helper function if Space is pressed, or start the game by changing to play mode if Enter is pressed. Add the highlighted lines.

    def on_key_down(key):
    if runner.mode == "play":
        if key == keys.SPACE and runner.y == GROUND:
            runner.speed_y = -15
    elif runner.mode == "game over":
        if key == keys.RETURN:
            reset()
    elif runner.mode == "costume":
        if key == keys.SPACE:
            change_costume()
        elif key == keys.RETURN:
            runner.mode = "play"

  6. One more thing: after a Game Over, the reset should send the player back to the costume screen. Make the highlighted update in reset().

    def reset():
    runner.score = 0
    runner.speed_y = 0
    obstacles.clear()
    runner.obstacles_timeout = 0
    runner.mode = "costume"

docs.title: Something You Should See
docs.text:
We're done with the game — but let's have a look at our two main functions, update() and draw():

def update():
    next_runner_image()
    if runner.mode == "play":
        apply_gravity()
        do_obstacles()
        runner.score += 1
        check_damage()

def draw():
    if runner.mode == "play":
        draw_game()
        draw_score()
    elif runner.mode == "game over":
        draw_game_over()
        draw_score()
    elif runner.mode == "costume":
        draw_costume()

Notice how small and tidy they are? Dividing our programs into many small functions lets us do bigger, more complex things. Consider how easy it would be to add a fourth mode to these two functions if we wanted it.

Let's also look at our draw_score() function:

def draw_score():
    screen.draw.text(f"Score: {runner.score}", (30, 30), color="white", fontsize=60)

Why did we make a whole function for a single line of code? Have another look at the draw() function above — we call draw_score() from two places. If you wanted to change the font or the color of the score, you would only need to update it in one place.

The takeaway

Functions are useful for:

  • Simplifying complex code.
  • Code reuse.

docs.title: Challenges
docs.text:
Try these on your own once the game works.

  • Make the obstacles appear at random times, so they aren't always spaced out the same.
  • Make the runner appear somewhere in the middle of the screen in costume mode, but in the correct location again during play mode.
  • Create a list of different obstacles, including the cactus, and randomly choose from it each time we add a new obstacle to the screen.

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text: • Submit your runner.py file in Google Classroom.

docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent All three modes work end to end: the costume screen cycles ninja, dino, and knight with Space and starts on Enter; the runner animates, jumps, and dodges timed cacti while the score climbs; Game Over keeps the final score on screen; and reset() puts everything back for the next round. Meanwhile update() and draw() stay short lists of helper calls — the actual point of the lab. 3 — Above Average All three modes work with a slip — a reset that forgets one thing (a lingering cactus, a score that carries over), or a costume that doesn't cycle back around. 2 — Average The game plays, but the mode system is incomplete — no costume screen, or no way back from Game Over. 1 — Below Average The runner animates and little else works. 0 — Failing Nothing submitted, or the program doesn't run.

docs.title: Actor Positioning and Platforms
