docs.title: How It's Graded
docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent The trees tile seamlessly across the bottom, weights fall from random spots with accelerate motion, each hit costs exactly one heart while the alien flashes its hit image through the invincibility countdown, and Game Over appears when the hearts run out. The whole chain works together. 3 — Above Average Everything is in place with a minor slip — weights falling linear instead of accelerating, or an invincibility window short enough that a slow weight double-dips. 2 — Average The background and falling weights work, but one hit drains every heart (no invincibility), or there's no Game Over screen. 1 — Below Average Little beyond the scene and the tiled background. 0 — Failing Nothing submitted, or the program doesn't run.

docs.title: Meet Reeborg!
docs.text: Reeborg is a robot who lives on a grid and does exactly what you tell it — no more, no less. That is the whole problem. Today you'll send Reeborg on a few short missions and find out just how literal a computer really is.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll learn the Python basics for controlling Reeborg — moving, turning, picking things up, and keeping your code readable — by solving a series of short missions.

Before you start

Each mission below has its own button that loads the right world. Save your work after every step — you'll turn all of them in at the end.

You've got it when…

  • Reeborg completes every mission: returns home, clears the dandelions, walks around the lake, and cleans up the gravel path.
  • Your code uses comments and blank lines so it's easy to read.
  • You've saved a .py file for every step.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. You can compare notes with a neighbor, but write your own commands.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: These missions are about learning to think like the robot. Write every command yourself this time. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Step 0 — Meet Reeborg
docs.text:
Open Step 0

We'll do this one together: playing and resetting Reeborg's world, adding a command, dealing with errors, using Reeborg's keyboard, and saving and loading your work.

docs.title: Step 1 — Return Home
docs.text:
Open Step 1

Your mission: give Reeborg the instructions to return home.

docs.title: Step 2 — Take and Put
docs.text:
Open Step 2

Use the take() function to pick an item up, and the put() function to set it down.

Your mission: pick up the dandelions, put them in the garbage, and return home.

docs.title: Step 3 — Turning
docs.text:
Open Step 3

Use the turn_left() function to make Reeborg turn left.

Your mission: make Reeborg walk around the lake.

docs.title: Step 4 — Comments and Whitespace
docs.text:
Open Step 4

Use comments to organize your code and make it easier to read. A comment is a note for humans that the computer ignores; it starts with the # symbol. Use whitespace — blank lines — the same way, to group your code into sections the computer also ignores.

# This is an example of
# a simple program where Reeborg draws a square,
# leaving an object behind at each corner.

# draw the first side
move()
move()
turn_left()
put()

# draw the second side
move()
move()
turn_left()
put()

# draw the third side
move()
turn_left()
put()

# draw the fourth side
move()
move()
turn_left()
put()

Use the pause() function to make Reeborg wait for you to click the play button.

Your mission: make Reeborg walk down the gravel path, picking up dandelions as it finds them and dropping them in the garbage cans (the grey dandelion images). Have Reeborg pause() at each dandelion it picks. Use comments and whitespace to keep your solution readable.

docs.text:
This lab is worth up to 4 points. One score covers everything you turn in.

Score What it looks like 4 — Excellent Reeborg completes all four missions — home, dandelions, lake, and the gravel path — your Step 4 code is organized with comments and blank lines like the example (with a pause() at each dandelion), and all five .py files are turned in. 3 — Above Average All five files are turned in and the missions work, with minor slips — a missing pause(), or comments that thin out near the end. 2 — Average Real gaps — a mission or two unfinished, files missing from the turn-in, or working code with no comments at all in Step 4. 1 — Below Average Largely incomplete — only one or two missions run, or most files were never saved. 0 — Failing Nothing turned in, or no evidence Reeborg ever moved.

docs.title: More Reeborg!
docs.text: Reeborg has no turn_right() function. It can only turn left, so a right turn takes three left turns — every single time. Instead of typing that over and over, you'll teach Reeborg the trick once by writing your own function, and reuse it forever.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll learn to define your own functions — reusable pieces of code with a name you choose — while you send Reeborg on new missions.

Before you start

Each mission below has its own button that loads the right world. Save your work after every step — you'll turn all of them in at the end.

You've got it when…

  • Your Step 4 solution turns right with one call to turn_right() wherever it used three turn_left() calls.
  • Your pick_two_berries() function is defined once and used four times to clear the garden.
  • You've saved a .py file for both steps.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. You can compare notes with a neighbor, but write your own commands.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: Writing your first functions yourself is the whole point of this one. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Step 4, Revisited — Your First Function
docs.text:
Open Step 4

You probably noticed that Reeborg has no function to turn right. It can only turn left, and we have to make three left turns to turn right.

We can create our own function. Functions are how we create pieces of code that we can reuse. We use the word def to define functions. Enter the following code at the top of your file:

def turn_right():
    turn_left()
    turn_left()
    turn_left()

Warning

The code that is part of your new turn_right() function must be indented. Use the Tab key to indent code.

Your mission: add the turn_right() function to the top of your Step 4.py file, then use it in your original solution to replace the places where Reeborg calls turn_left() three times to make a right turn.

docs.title: Step 5 — The Strawberry Garden
docs.text:
Open Step 5

Your mission: write code to pick all the strawberries from the rows in the garden and put them on the ground in the center.

Define a pick_two_berries() function that picks up two strawberries and puts them on the ground. Use it four times as part of your solution.

Tip

Assume that your function starts with Reeborg standing in the center and facing a row of two strawberries.

docs.title: Turn It In
docs.text:
Turn in your Python (.py) file for each step:

  • Step 4.py
  • Step 5.py

Careful!

Your new Step 4.py might have a slightly different name if your Step 4 solution from the previous assignment is still in your Downloads folder. Be sure to turn in the newest one for this assignment.

Credit: Adapted from Dan Schellenberg's Computer Science 20 textbook.

docs.title: Even More Reeborg!
docs.text: You wrote a handy turn_right() function last time — and then had to copy and paste it into your next program. There is a better way: put it in a library once, and every program you write from now on can borrow it. Then you'll teach Reeborg to answer questions about the world around it and act on the answers.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll learn to share functions between programs with a library, and to use if statements with Reeborg's built-in sensing functions so your program can make decisions on its own.

Before you start

Each mission below has its own button that loads the right world. Save your work after every step — you'll turn all of them in at the end.

You've got it when…

  • Your library holds turn_right() and turn_around(), and your Step 6 program imports and uses them to put the star inside the house.
  • Your Step 8 program finds every flower on its own — no matter where they are — puts them on the grey flowers, and returns to the flag.
  • You've saved a .py file for both steps.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. You can compare notes with a neighbor, but write your own commands.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: These missions are about learning to think like the robot. Write every command yourself this time. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Step 6 — Build a Library
docs.text:
Open Step 6

We made a handy new turn_right() function in Step 4. You might have even copied and pasted it to Step 5.

We'll probably want to be able to turn right in a lot of programs we write. When we want to share code with multiple programs, we can add it to a library.

Below are two functions, turn_right() from before and a new function called turn_around(). Let's put them in a library and make them available to all our future programs.

def turn_right():
    turn_left()
    turn_left()
    turn_left()

def turn_around():
    turn_left()
    turn_left()

  1. Copy and paste the code above into the library tab.

  2. Switch back to the Python Code tab.

  3. Add this line to the top of your file. It must be on line 1!

    import library

When we want to use these functions in a new program, we must first import the library. This tells Python which library we want to use. Then we can use the library functions in our program, but we must add the word library. before the name of each function we want to use. For example, to use the turn_right() function, we would write:

library.turn_right()

Your mission: make Reeborg pick up the star from the lawn outside its house and set it down inside the house. Use the new turn_right() and turn_around() functions from the library in your program.

docs.title: Step 8 — Asking Questions
docs.text:
Open Step 8

Reeborg can call some functions to ask questions about its environment. Each is a "yes" or "no" question — each function returns either True or False.

Function What it answers at_goal() Returns True if Reeborg is on a goal tile (flag, home, or green tile), False otherwise. front_is_clear() Returns True if there is no obstacle (wall, etc.) in front of Reeborg, False otherwise. right_is_clear() Returns True if there is no obstacle (wall, etc.) to the right of Reeborg, False otherwise. wall_in_front() Returns True if there is a wall in front of Reeborg, False otherwise. wall_on_right() Returns True if there is a wall on the right side of Reeborg, False otherwise. object_here() Returns True if there is an object (star, dandelion, etc.) on the same tile Reeborg is standing on, False otherwise. carries_object() Returns True if Reeborg is carrying at least one object, False if Reeborg is carrying nothing. is_facing_north() Returns True if Reeborg is currently facing north, False otherwise.

We can use an if to ask these questions and take actions based on whether the answer is True or False:

if front_is_clear():
    move()

Warning

Notice the colon (:) at the end of the if line!

Your mission: the flowers in this world change positions every time it is played, so we can't know ahead of time where the flowers will be.

  • Use the functions above to ask questions and make Reeborg find and collect all the flowers as it walks along the yard from left to right. After each move, if there is an object there, pick it up.
  • Put all the flowers down on grid space (2, 3), which is the grey flowers.
  • Return to the checkered flag at grid space (1, 3).

docs.text:

docs.title: More Reeborg! MORE REEBORG!
docs.text: Typing move() eight times in a row works, but it should bother you a little. Computers exist to repeat things so we don't have to. Today you'll hand the repetition to a loop and keep the interesting parts for yourself.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll learn to repeat instructions with loops and combine them with your own functions — first to tighten up an old solution, then to send Reeborg over a row of hurdles.

Before you start

Each mission below has its own button that loads the right world. Save your work after every step — you'll turn all of them in at the end.

You've got it when…

  • Your Step 8 solution uses at least two loops and still completes the mission.
  • Your jump_hurdle() function clears one hurdle, and a loop calls it to clear them all.
  • You've saved a .py file for both steps.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. You can compare notes with a neighbor, but write your own commands.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: These missions are about learning to think like the robot. Write every command yourself this time. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Step 9 — Loops
docs.text:
Open Step 9

Sometimes we need to repeat instructions several times. Instead of writing out each repeated instruction like this:

move()
move()
move()
move()
move()
move()
move()
move()

…we can instead use a loop, like this:

repeat 8:
    move()

Your mission: update your solution from Step 8 to use at least two loops. You can use loops in your Python code and also in your library!

docs.title: Step 10 — Hurdles
docs.text:
Open Step 10

Your mission:

  1. Create a new function named jump_hurdle() that jumps a single hurdle. Here's some code to get started.

    def jump_hurdle():
    # your code goes here

  2. Use a loop to call your jump_hurdle() function repeatedly to jump all the hurdles.

docs.title: Reeborg, the REEBORGANING!
docs.text: So far your if statements do something when the answer is yes and nothing when the answer is no. Real decisions have two branches: turn at the corner or keep walking. Today Reeborg learns else — and its first real Python loop.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll learn to handle both sides of a decision with if/else, and to keep a program running as long as a condition holds with a while loop.

Before you start

Each mission below has its own button that loads the right world. Save your work after every step — you'll turn all of them in at the end.

You've got it when…

  • Reeborg walks the whole yard and gathers the corner flowers no matter what size the yard is.
  • Reeborg carries every apple to the compost bin without knowing the count ahead of time.
  • You've saved a .py file for both steps.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. You can compare notes with a neighbor, but write your own commands.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: These missions are about learning to think like the robot. Write every command yourself this time. What the levels mean.

docs.title: Step 11 — if and else
docs.text:
Open Step 11

We've already seen how to use if in our programs. Now we'll add a new piece: else.

if and else work together like this:

if it_rains():
    keep_reading()
else:
    go_outside_and_play()

Your mission: make Reeborg walk around the outside of the yard gathering flowers from each corner. The length and width of the yard changes each time the program is started, but we know that it will take exactly 23 steps to walk completely around the yard every time. Use both if and else to determine when to turn at a corner or walk straight.

docs.title: Step 12 — The while Loop
docs.text:
Open Step 12

Now we'll see one of the real kinds of loops that is available in all Python programs (remember, repeat is only available for Reeborg!).

A while loop does something for as long as a condition is true. It looks like this:

while front_is_clear():
    move()

Your mission: make Reeborg take the apples from the house to the compost bin outside. We don't know ahead of time how many apples are stacked up in the house. Use a while loop to continue picking them up until there are none left to bring outside.

docs.title: ULTIMATE Reeborg!
docs.text: One mission. Any maze. Reeborg starts anywhere, the goal could be anywhere, and your program has to solve it every time. Everything you've learned — functions, conditionals, and loops — comes together here.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You'll learn two final pieces of Python decision-making — elif and not — and use them to write a program that can solve any maze Reeborg is dropped into.

Before you start

The mission below has a button that loads the world. Save your work — you'll turn it in at the end.

You've got it when…

  • Reeborg reaches the goal no matter where it starts and no matter where the goal is.
  • Your solution uses a while loop with not, and if/elif/else.
  • You've saved your .py file.

Collaboration & AI

Work: On your own. You can compare notes with a neighbor, but write your own commands.

AI — AIAS Level 1, No AI: This is the final boss. Beat it yourself. What the levels mean.

docs.title: if/elif/else
docs.text:
We have seen how if and else work together. Let's add one more piece: "else if", written elif, works like this:

if it_rains():
    play_indoors()
elif it_snows():
    go_skiing()
else:
    go_swimming() # assuming it is warm!

docs.title: not
docs.text:
Sometimes we want to ask if something is not true. The Python not keyword works like this:

if not is_raining():
    open_windows()

not can also be used in a while loop:

while not glass_full():
    pour_milk()

docs.title: Your Mission
docs.text:
Open Step 17

Help Reeborg solve the maze, regardless of where it starts or where the goal is!

You must use a while loop with a not, and if/elif/else. Here's how:

  • while Reeborg is not at the goal:
    • if the way is clear to the right, turn right and move forward
    • else, if the way is clear to the front, move forward
    • else turn left

Why keep a hand on the wall?

This strategy is called wall following: keep your right hand on the wall and walk, and in a maze like this one you will eventually reach the goal. People use it in real corn mazes. It is slower than knowing the way — but Reeborg doesn't know the way, and neither do you.

Criteria Emerging Developing Proficient Distinguished Creativity & Innovation Response lacks creativity and does not explore new ideas. Response shows some creativity but lacks depth or originality. Response is creative and presents a solid, well-considered idea. Response demonstrates original, imaginative thinking with a unique and thought-provoking perspective. Response is clearly written, well-structured, and easy to follow. Ideas flow logically. Depth & Justification Response lacks justification or explanation. Response provides detailed reasoning and strong justification for the proposed solution. Engagement with the Prompt Shows little engagement with the question; response is superficial or incomplete. Partially engages with the question but does not fully explore its implications. Engages with the question and presents a reasonable response. Fully engages with the question, exploring its implications and offering insightful ideas.

docs.title: Scale
docs.text:
1

NO AI 

The assessment is completed entirely without AI assistance in a controlled environment, ensuring that students rely solely on their existing knowledge, understanding, and skills

You must not use AI at any point during the assessment. You must demonstrate your core skills and knowledge.

2

AI PLANNING 

AI may be used for pre-task activities such as brainstorming, outlining and initial research. This level focuses on the effective use of AI for planning, synthesis, and ideation, but assessments should emphasise the ability to develop and refine these ideas independently.

You may use AI for planning, idea development, and research. Your final submission should show how you have developed and refined these ideas.

3

AI COLLABORATION

AI may be used to help complete the task, including idea generation, drafting, feedback, and refinement. Students should critically evaluate and modify the AI suggested outputs, demonstrating their understanding.

You may use AI to assist with specific tasks such as drafting text, refining and evaluating your work. You must critically evaluate and modify any AI-generated content you use.

4

FULL AI 

AI may be used to complete any elements of the task, with students directing AI to achieve the assessment goals. Assessments at this level may also require engagement with AI to achieve goals and solve problems.

You may use AI extensively throughout your work either as you wish, or as specifically directed in your assessment. Focus on directing AI to achieve your goals while demonstrating your critical thinking.

5

AI EXPLORATION 

AI is used creatively to enhance problem-solving, generate novel insights, or develop innovative solutions to solve problems. Students and educators co-design assessments to explore unique AI applications within the field of study.

You should use AI creatively to solve the task, potentially co-designing new approaches with your instructor.
